dpia.title: Do you need a data protection impact assessment?
dpia.tag: An assessment identifies privacy risks before a project starts. Check the EU and UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requirements.
dpia.nodes.q-role.q: Do you decide why and how the personal data is used?
dpia.nodes.q-role.help: The controller is the organization that decides why and how personal data is used. Article 35(1) makes the controller responsible for the impact assessment. A processor handles data on the controller’s behalf and must help with the assessment. The same allocation applies under the UK GDPR.
dpia.nodes.q-role.opts.0.label: Yes — we make those decisions alone or jointly with another organization
dpia.nodes.q-role.opts.1.label: No — we only handle data on another organization’s instructions
dpia.nodes.o-processor.title: The controller must do the assessment; you must help
dpia.nodes.q-types.q: Does the activity fall into one of these categories in Article 35(3)?
dpia.nodes.q-types.help: These three categories require a data protection impact assessment under both the EU and UK GDPR. Your data protection regulator may also require assessments for other activities listed under Article 35(4). In the UK, check the Information Commissioner’s Office list of examples of processing likely to result in high risk.
dpia.nodes.q-other-risk.q: How many of these nine privacy risk factors apply?
dpia.nodes.q-other-risk.help: EU guidance WP248 lists nine factors: evaluating or scoring people; automated decisions with significant effects; systematic monitoring; sensitive or highly personal data; large-scale use; matching or combining datasets; people who are especially vulnerable; new uses of technology; and processing that prevents people from exercising a right or using a service or contract. Two or more factors usually call for an assessment, but one can be enough. In the UK, follow the Information Commissioner’s Office guidance and Article 35(4) list. The EU guidance can help explain the issue, but it does not bind the UK regulator.
dpia.nodes.q-other-risk.opts.0.label: Two or more of the nine factors apply
dpia.nodes.q-sa-list.q: Does your data protection regulator list this activity as requiring an impact assessment?
dpia.nodes.q-sa-list.help: Check the current list published under Article 35(4). Some listed activities require an assessment on their own, without a second risk factor. For example, the UK list includes matching datasets and targeting children or other vulnerable people. Several EU regulators have comparable entries. Lists can change, so check the current version for the relevant country.
dpia.nodes.o-dpia-presumed.title: An assessment is usually needed — document any decision not to do one
dpia.nodes.o-dpia-presumed.summary: Two or more WP248 risk factors usually mean an assessment is needed under Article 35(1). This is guidance, rather than an automatic legal requirement under Article 35(3). You may decide an assessment is unnecessary if you can clearly document why. A listed activity under your regulator’s Article 35(4) list is different: an assessment is then mandatory. In the UK, apply the Information Commissioner’s Office guidance and list; WP248 does not bind the UK regulator.
dpia.nodes.o-dpia-presumed.actions.1: Check the current Article 35(4) list from your regulator. If the activity meets an entry, you must do the assessment.
dpia.nodes.o-dpia-recommended.title: An assessment is strongly recommended, even if it is not mandatory
dpia.nodes.o-dpia-recommended.summary: One WP248 factor does not automatically require an assessment, but a single factor can sometimes be enough. This result assumes the activity is not on the regulator’s Article 35(4) mandatory list. An assessment can still help you identify risks and demonstrate compliance with Articles 5(2) and 24.
dpia.nodes.o-dpia-not-required.actions.0: Record which risk factors you considered and why the activity is unlikely to create a high risk.
dpia.nodes.q-sa-list-none.q: Does your data protection regulator list this activity as requiring an impact assessment?
dpia.nodes.q-sa-list-none.help: Check the current list published under Article 35(4). Some listed activities require an assessment on their own, without a second risk factor. For example, the UK list includes matching datasets and targeting children or other vulnerable people. Several EU regulators have comparable entries. Lists can change, so check the current version for the relevant country.

dpo.title: Do you need a data protection officer?
dpo.tag: A data protection officer advises on privacy obligations and monitors compliance. Check the EU and UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) appointment rules.
dpo.nodes.q-public.help: Article 37(1)(a) requires public authorities and public bodies to appoint a data protection officer, except courts when deciding cases. National law can add requirements for private organizations; Germany’s Federal Data Protection Act, section 38, is one example. Article 37(1) applies to processors as well as controllers: if you handle data for clients, answer the later questions about the core activities you carry out for them.
dpo.nodes.q-monitoring.help: Article 37(1)(b) applies when monitoring people on a large scale is a core activity: work essential to what your organization does, rather than support work such as internal human resources. Monitoring includes tracking and profiling. To assess scale, consider how many people are affected, how much data is used, how long the activity lasts and its geographic reach. Guidance WP243 gives examples including app location tracking, behavioral advertising, loyalty programs and public-space surveillance cameras.
dpo.nodes.q-special-large.q: Is using sensitive data or criminal-conviction data on a large scale a core activity?
dpo.nodes.q-special-large.help: Article 37(1)(c) covers large-scale use of special category data under Article 9, such as health information, and criminal-conviction data under Article 10. Hospitals, insurers and large research institutions are common examples. Guidance WP243 considers the number or proportion of people affected, the volume of data, the duration and geographic reach.
dpo.nodes.q-local-law.q: Does the relevant country’s law require a data protection officer for your sector or organization size?
dpo.nodes.o-dpo-req.actions.3: Check whether the officer’s other responsibilities conflict with this role. X-FAB (C-453/21) says a conflict may arise when those responsibilities include deciding why and how personal data is used. Assess the actual duties; common examples include a chief information officer or a head of human resources or compliance.
dpo.nodes.o-dpo-req.actions.5: Have the officer report directly to the highest level of management (Article 38(3)).
dpo.nodes.o-voluntary.title: A voluntarily appointed officer has the same duties and protections
dpo.nodes.o-voluntary.summary: The WP243 guidance says that a formally appointed data protection officer must meet Articles 38–39 even when the appointment is voluntary. If you want a privacy lead without making that formal appointment, use a different title and do not designate that person as the data protection officer.
dpo.nodes.o-no-dpo.title: You do not have to appoint a data protection officer
dpo.nodes.o-no-dpo.summary: You must still be able to show that the organization complies with data protection law under Articles 5(2) and 24. That responsibility does not, by itself, require you to appoint an officer.
dpo.nodes.o-no-dpo.actions.2: Consider assigning a privacy lead. This does not need to be a formal data protection officer appointment under Articles 38–39.
dpo.nodes.o-court.summary: Article 37(1)(a) excludes courts when acting in their judicial role, to protect judicial independence. The exception does not cover a court’s administrative work, for which a data protection officer is still required.

ropa.title: Do you need records of how you use personal data?
ropa.tag: Check the EU and UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requirements for written records of processing activities.
ropa.q: Which activities must you record, and what must the records include?
ropa.nodes.q-size.help: Article 30(5) generally exempts organizations with fewer than 250 employees, but three exceptions can still require records. Organizations with 250 or more employees must keep them. An EU proposal from May 2025 would change the threshold to fewer than 750 employees and limit the exceptions to processing likely to create a high risk. The source review recorded that it had not been adopted as of mid-2026; check its current status if this affects you. The EU proposal does not change the UK’s 250-employee threshold.
ropa.nodes.q-small-exceptions.help: Even with fewer than 250 employees, you must keep records for activities that are likely to create a risk to people’s rights, occur regularly rather than occasionally, or involve sensitive or criminal-conviction data. Under the Article 29 Working Party’s 19 April 2018 Position Paper on Article 30(5), the duty covers the activities meeting those conditions. It does not automatically cover every activity in the organization. The paper treats an activity as occasional only if it is not carried out regularly and falls outside the regular course of business. Its example: a small organization’s regular processing of employee data is not occasional, so payroll, staff records and ongoing customer records normally must be recorded.
ropa.nodes.q-small-exceptions.opts.1.label: The activity happens regularly, rather than occasionally
ropa.nodes.q-small-exceptions.opts.2.label: The activity uses sensitive data under Article 9 or criminal-conviction data under Article 10
ropa.nodes.o-required.title: Keep written records of the relevant processing activities
ropa.nodes.o-required.summary: The records must be written; electronic records are permitted (Article 30(3)). You must give them to the relevant data protection regulator on request (Article 30(4)). They help demonstrate compliance under Article 5(2) and are commonly requested during investigations.
ropa.nodes.o-required.actions.2: If you act as a controller for some activities and a processor for others, keep both types of record under Articles 30(1) and 30(2).
ropa.nodes.o-required.actions.3: Update the records when the way you use personal data changes.
ropa.nodes.o-not-required.title: These records are not mandatory, but a short register is recommended
ropa.nodes.o-not-required.summary: This result is uncommon: most organizations with staff or regular customers keep at least some records. A short register of your main activities, legal grounds and retention periods can help you show compliance with Article 5(2), even when Article 30 does not require records. It also helps you prepare if your organization later crosses a threshold.
ropa.nodes.o-not-required.actions.1: Check the threshold each year and when the activity changes. Reaching 250 employees, or beginning regular processing, can create a record-keeping duty.
ropa.nodes.q-small-exceptions.opts.3.label: None of the above: no payroll, staff or ongoing customer records, only one-off, low-risk activities without sensitive data

legal-basis.title: What allows you to use this personal data?
legal-basis.tag: Choose a legal ground under Article 6 of the EU or UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and check the conditions it requires.
legal-basis.q: Which legal ground applies, and what does it require?
legal-basis.nodes.q-purpose.q: Why do you need to use the personal data?
legal-basis.nodes.q-purpose.help: Article 6(1) lists the legal grounds for using personal data. Choose the ground that fits the actual activity. Each has its own conditions and affects the rights people can exercise, including deletion under Article 17 and receiving a portable copy under Article 20. Your privacy notice must explain the ground you use.
legal-basis.nodes.q-li-or-consent.q: Will you rely on a documented legitimate interest, or ask for consent?
legal-basis.nodes.q-li-or-consent.help: Legitimate interests means you have a lawful reason for the activity, need the data to carry it out, and have balanced that reason against the person’s rights. Document all three parts of that assessment (Article 6(1)(f)). Consent is the alternative under Article 6(1)(a): the person must understand a specific choice, make it freely and clearly, and be able to withdraw as easily as they agreed (Articles 4(11) and 7). The appropriate choice depends on the activity and its effect on people.
legal-basis.nodes.q-li-or-consent.opts.0.label: We have completed the assessment and can rely on legitimate interests
legal-basis.nodes.q-li-or-consent.opts.2.label: Either could work, and people would expect to be asked for consent
legal-basis.nodes.q-li-or-consent.opts.3.label: Either could work, but asking for consent is impractical, such as for fraud prevention
legal-basis.nodes.o-contract.title: Use the contract ground only for data the contract actually needs
legal-basis.nodes.o-contract.actions.2: Do not treat marketing, analytics or behavioral advertising as necessary for a contract. Assess a separate legal ground, such as legitimate interests or consent. Separately, storing or reading information on a device (cookies, pixels, software development kits) needs consent under ePrivacy rules unless an exception applies (Planet49 (C-673/17)).
legal-basis.nodes.o-vital.title: Protect someone’s life or other vital interests
legal-basis.nodes.o-public-task.title: Carry out a task in the public interest or exercise official authority
legal-basis.nodes.o-li.title: You can rely on legitimate interests, subject to its conditions
legal-basis.nodes.o-li.actions.4: Give particular weight to children’s rights when balancing interests. Article 6(1)(f) specifically calls for that protection.
legal-basis.nodes.o-consent.title: Obtain valid consent before using the data
legal-basis.nodes.o-consent.actions.2: Make withdrawal as easy as giving consent, and clearly show people how to withdraw.
legal-basis.nodes.o-consent.actions.4: EU Article 8 sets a default digital-consent age of 16, but each EU country may set an age from 13 to 16. Check the applicable national law. The UK age is 13 under Data Protection Act 2018 section 9. Below the applicable age, obtain parental authorization.
legal-basis.nodes.o-legal-obligation.actions.1: Foreign legal obligations (for example, US subpoenas) are not a valid Article 6(1)(c) ground. EU: see Article 48 and European Data Protection Board Guidelines 02/2024 on Article 48 (final version adopted 5 June 2025). UK: the analysis runs through the UK GDPR’s own transfer regime (UK GDPR Articles 44–49, International Data Transfer Agreement / UK adequacy regulations), not Court of Justice authority.
legal-basis.nodes.o-li.actions.0: Conduct and document a three-part legitimate interests assessment: (1) legitimate interest, (2) necessity, (3) balancing. For EU processing, use European Data Protection Board Guidelines 1/2024; only the October 2024 consultation version had been published as of October 2026. Court of Justice C-621/22 KNLTB confirms purely commercial interests can qualify.
legal-basis.nodes.q-purpose.opts.0.label: We need it to perform a contract with the person, or take steps they requested before a contract

role.title: Are you a controller or a processor?
role.tag: A controller decides why and how personal data is used. A processor handles it on the controller’s behalf. Check your role under the EU or UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
role.q: Who makes the decisions about this use of personal data?
role.nodes.q-decides.help: A controller decides why personal data is used and the important details of how it is used (Article 4(7)). A processor handles it on the controller’s behalf (Article 4(8)). Important decisions include the types of data, retention periods and recipients. A processor can choose technical tools without becoming the controller. EU guidance explains this distinction in Guidelines 07/2020. In the UK, use the Information Commissioner’s Office controller and processor guidance; EU guidance is not binding there after Brexit.
role.nodes.q-means.q: Do you also decide what data is used, how long it is kept and who receives it?
role.nodes.q-means.help: These important decisions are called the essential means of processing. Choosing servers or other technical tools can be delegated to a processor without changing roles. Because you decide why the data is used, you are already acting as a controller. This question checks whether another organization shares control over the same activity.
role.nodes.q-on-behalf.q: Do you have the written data processing agreement required by Article 28?
role.nodes.q-on-behalf.help: Article 28(3) requires a contract or other binding legal agreement between the controller and processor. Your actual work can still make you a processor when the agreement is missing, but the missing agreement is a compliance failure.
role.nodes.q-on-behalf.opts.0.label: Yes — the Article 28 agreement has all required terms
role.nodes.q-on-behalf.opts.1.label: There is no agreement, or required terms are missing
role.nodes.q-on-behalf.opts.2.label: There is an agreement, but we sometimes act beyond the controller’s instructions
role.nodes.q-beyond.help: You become a controller for an activity when you decide its purposes and important methods beyond the controller’s instructions (Article 28(10)). Departing only from instructions about technical details, timing or execution can breach Article 28(3)(a) without changing your role.
role.nodes.o-joint.actions.3: Each responsible controller may be liable for the full compensation owed for damage under Article 82(2)–(4).
role.nodes.o-processor-ok.title: You are a processor with the required data processing agreement
role.nodes.o-processor-ok.actions.2: Do not use the data for your own purposes. That can make you the controller for that activity under Article 28(10).
role.nodes.o-processor-ok.actions.3: Get the controller’s authorization before appointing another processor, and include the required Article 28 duties in that processor’s contract.
role.nodes.o-processor-gap.title: You are a processor, but the required agreement is missing or incomplete
role.nodes.o-processor-gap.summary: Article 28(3) requires a compliant agreement. Both the controller and processor can breach that requirement by processing without one. Spain’s data protection regulator has fined both parties in such cases.
role.nodes.o-processor-gap.actions.2: Correct the agreement and document the earlier failure accurately. Do not backdate it to conceal the problem.
role.nodes.o-controller-by-default.title: You are a controller for the activities you decide for yourself
role.nodes.o-instruction-breach.title: You remain a processor, but have breached the controller’s instructions
role.nodes.o-instruction-breach.summary: Acting outside documented instructions breaches Article 28(3)(a) and your data processing agreement. If the departure concerns only technical or execution details, it does not by itself make you a controller. If you decide the purposes or important methods for that activity, Article 28(10) can make you its controller. Your actual decisions determine the role, regardless of the contract’s label.
role.nodes.o-multi-role.title: You are a controller for some activities and a processor for others
role.nodes.o-multi-role.summary: Assess each activity separately. For example, a software provider may process customer-uploaded data on the customer’s instructions, but act as controller for its own billing or product-improvement activities. Guidelines 07/2020 recognize that one organization can have both roles.
role.nodes.o-controller.summary:
You decide why personal data is used and the essential parts of how it is used. You are responsible for the duties that apply to a controller, including the Article 5 principles, an Article 6 legal ground, people’s rights under Articles 12–22, the Article 30 processing record, Article 33 breach reporting, Article 35 impact assessments and privacy information.

In the UK, read the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The amended automated-decision rules are in Articles 22A–22D, alongside the rights in Articles 12–21. The 2025 Act also provides for reasonable and proportionate searches when answering access requests, pauses to the response period while awaiting requested clarification, and recognized legitimate interests. Its provisions start in stages, so check which are in force on your assessment date and the current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance.
role.nodes.o-controller.actions.3: Take responsibility for responding to people’s rights requests. In the UK, apply the reasonable and proportionate search rule and any permitted pause while awaiting clarification under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
role.nodes.o-controller-by-default.summary: If a processor goes beyond the controller’s instructions and decides why and how data is used, Article 28(10) makes it a controller for that use. European Data Protection Board Guidelines 07/2020 focus on actual decisions, regardless of what the contract calls the parties. For example, a vendor may become a controller if it uses customer data to train its own AI model without the controller’s instruction.
role.nodes.q-means.opts.2.label: Another organization decides the essential means (data types, retention, recipients) for its own purposes
role.nodes.q-means.opts.2.resultNotes.0: Two parties each influencing the processing for their own purposes points to joint control, not a controller-processor relationship (European Data Protection Board Guidelines 07/2020).
role.nodes.o-joint.summary: Article 26: where two or more controllers jointly determine purposes and means, they are joint controllers and must agree a transparent arrangement dividing their responsibilities between them, in particular for people’s rights. The essence of the arrangement must be made available to the person whose data you use. The Court of Justice trio, Wirtschaftsakademie (C-210/16), Jehovan todistajat (C-25/17) and Fashion ID (C-40/17), established that joint controllership can arise from even limited shared decision-making, but only for the stages decided jointly. IAB Europe (C-604/22) held that an industry-framework operator can be a joint controller where, in the circumstances, it influences the processing for its own purposes, and that this does not automatically extend to later processing by others. European Data Protection Board Guidelines 07/2020 codify the doctrine. UK note: post-2020 Court of Justice judgments (including IAB Europe) and European Data Protection Board guidance are persuasive, not binding, under the UK GDPR; the pre-2021 trio is assimilated case law from which UK higher courts may now depart under the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023. The Information Commissioner’s Office controller and processor guidance is the UK reference.
role.nodes.o-joint.actions.6: If you operate an industry consent framework: in the EU you can be a joint controller for the consent-recording stage where you influence it for your own purposes; that status does not automatically cover later processing by participants (IAB Europe (C-604/22)). In the UK that ruling is not binding; the same result is likely under UK GDPR Article 4(7) first principles, but it is not settled. Check current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance.

cookies.title: Do these cookies or tracking tools need consent?
cookies.tag: Check EU cookie rules and the UK Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, alongside the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
cookies.q: Must you ask permission before using this tracking technology?
cookies.nodes.q-storage.q: Does the technology store information on a person’s device, or read information already there?
cookies.nodes.q-storage.help: The rule covers more than cookies. It can apply to browser storage, tracking pixels that read information, software development kits and device fingerprinting. Guidelines 2/2023 also cover tracking through links, connected devices and inserted identifiers. IP-address tracking or purely local processing is covered when the server instructs the device to send or produce identifying data. Planet49 (C-673/17) confirms the broad EU scope. In the UK, regulation 6 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations applies, as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. EU guidance can help explain the issue but does not bind the UK regulator.
cookies.nodes.q-storage.opts.0.label: Yes — it uses cookies, browser storage, device fingerprinting or similar access
cookies.nodes.q-storage.opts.1.label: No — there is no device storage or read access, such as server-only analytics with no device identifiers
cookies.nodes.o-no-eprivacy.title: The device-access consent rule does not apply; data protection law may still apply
cookies.nodes.o-no-eprivacy.summary: If the technology does not store information on a device or read it, the EU ePrivacy Article 5(3) rule does not apply. Using personal data still needs an Article 6 legal ground. IP addresses are usually personal data when identification is reasonably possible (Breyer, C-582/14). Check the technical design: Guidelines 2/2023 say even IP-only tracking can fall within Article 5(3) when the server instructs the device to send identifying data.
cookies.nodes.q-strictly-nec.q: Is the device access essential to transmit a communication or provide the service the person requested?
cookies.nodes.q-strictly-nec.help: Article 5(3) allows two exceptions: access used solely to transmit a communication, and access strictly necessary to provide a service the person explicitly requested. Examples include login authentication, shopping carts, load balancing, security tokens and keeping user input during a session. Opinion 04/2012 (WP194) and Guidelines 2/2023 explain the exceptions. A business or vendor preference alone is not enough. UK: since 5 February 2026, Schedule A1 paragraph 4 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations lists examples of strictly necessary purposes, including protecting the service or device, preventing or detecting fraud or technical faults, automatically authenticating the user and recording what the user selects or enters.
cookies.nodes.q-strictly-nec.opts.0.label: Yes — it is essential for the requested service, such as login, a cart or necessary security
cookies.nodes.q-strictly-nec.opts.1.label: We prefer to use it, but the person’s requested service does not need it
cookies.nodes.o-strictly-nec.title: Consent is not required for this strictly necessary use
cookies.nodes.q-purpose.help: In the EU, non-exempt device storage or access needs consent under ePrivacy Article 5(3). Legitimate interests cannot replace that consent. If personal data is used, Article 6(1)(a) also applies. The UK has separate statutory exceptions for specified statistical and appearance or functionality purposes; the following questions distinguish those cases.
cookies.nodes.q-analytics-juris.q: Are you assessing analytics for people in the EU or wider European Economic Area, or in the UK?
cookies.nodes.o-analytics.title: EU: ask for consent unless a narrow national analytics exception applies
cookies.nodes.o-analytics-uk.title: UK: specified statistical cookies may use the notice-and-opt-out exception
cookies.nodes.o-analytics-uk.actions.3: The Data (Use and Access) Act raises cookie-rule penalties from the former £500,000 cap to UK GDPR levels.
cookies.nodes.o-advertising.title: EU and UK: obtain consent for advertising cookies
cookies.nodes.q-functionality-juris.q: Are you assessing personalization for people in the EU or wider European Economic Area, or in the UK?
cookies.nodes.o-functionality.title: EU: obtain consent for nonessential personalization or experiments
cookies.nodes.o-functionality.actions.1: Give separate consent choices for different purposes.
cookies.nodes.o-functionality.actions.3: Provide a clear way to withdraw consent, such as a permanent settings link.
cookies.nodes.o-functionality-uk.title: UK: adapting the service to the user’s preferences may qualify for an exception
cookies.nodes.o-analytics.actions.4: Make rejecting cookies as easy as accepting them. Put a reject option on the first screen of the banner, with no more steps than acceptance, following the French regulator’s Google decision SAN-2021-023.
cookies.nodes.o-advertising.actions.2: Make rejecting cookies as easy as accepting them, with a reject option on the first screen and no extra steps. Sources: the French regulator’s Google decision SAN-2021-023; the European Data Protection Board’s January 2023 Cookie Banner Taskforce report; and the Information Commissioner’s Office’s November 2023 cookie-banner initiative.
cookies.nodes.q-functionality-juris.help: The EU and UK diverged in 2025. EU: functionality and personalization beyond strictly-necessary require consent under Article 5(3). UK: Schedule A1 paragraph 6 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations allows storage or access whose sole purpose is adapting the service’s appearance or functionality to the user’s preferences, or otherwise enhancing them, on a notice-plus-objection basis, in force since 5 February 2026. A/B testing is not named in the UK exceptions; whether it fits depends on its sole purpose.
cookies.nodes.o-functionality.summary: A/B testing, recommendation algorithms and personalization beyond what is strictly necessary all need consent in the EU. Do not set the cookie before consent is captured. UK note: A/B testing is not named in the Schedule A1 exceptions. Testing whose sole purpose is collecting statistics on how the service is used, to improve it, may fit the statistical exception (paragraph 5) if the information is shared only for that purpose and users get clear information and a free, simple way to object. Testing tied to advertising, marketing or profiling individuals needs consent. Genuine user-preference personalization for UK users may fit the UK branch instead.
cookies.nodes.o-functionality-uk.summary: Schedule A1 paragraph 6 of the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, allows storage or access whose sole purpose is adapting the service’s appearance or functionality to the user’s preferences, or otherwise enhancing them, on a notice-plus-objection basis rather than prior consent. The exceptions have been in force since 5 February 2026; the Information Commissioner’s Office final storage and access guidance (29 April 2026) is the operative reference. A/B testing is not named: it may fit only where its sole purpose fits paragraph 5 or 6.
cookies.nodes.o-functionality-uk.actions.2: For A/B testing and experimentation, confirm the sole purpose. Usage statistics to improve the service may fit paragraph 5; anything tied to advertising, marketing or profiling individuals needs prior consent.

transfer.title: Can you transfer personal data to another country?
transfer.tag: Check the legal requirements for transfers outside the European Economic Area under the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or outside the UK under the UK GDPR.
transfer.q: Is the transfer permitted, and what safeguards do you need?
transfer.nodes.q-destination.q: Will a recipient outside the European Economic Area receive or access EU-regulated data, or a recipient outside the UK receive or access UK-regulated data?
transfer.nodes.q-destination.help: Chapter 5 requires a legal basis for an international transfer. Making data available can count even if you do not send a copy. For example, remote access by a recipient in another country can be a transfer. EU Guidelines 05/2021 explain how Article 3 and Chapter 5 interact.
transfer.nodes.q-destination.opts.0.label: Yes — a recipient outside the relevant area receives or can access the data
transfer.nodes.q-destination.opts.1.label: No — all processing stays within the relevant European Economic Area or UK boundary
transfer.nodes.q-destination.opts.2.label: Yes — our European Economic Area processor uses another processor outside that area
transfer.nodes.o-no-transfer.title: No international transfer safeguard is needed under Chapter 5
transfer.nodes.o-no-transfer.actions.2: Reassess if the provider changes where its other processors are located.
transfer.nodes.q-adequacy.q: Has the EU or UK formally approved the destination’s level of data protection?
transfer.nodes.q-safeguard.q: Can you use one of the safeguards allowed by Article 46?
transfer.nodes.q-safeguard.help: Article 46 allows safeguards including standard contractual clauses, approved rules for transfers within a corporate group, approved codes or certifications with binding commitments, and individually approved contract terms. The 2021 EU standard contractual clauses contain versions for the different controller and processor relationships. EU transfers also need an assessment of protection in the destination following Schrems II (C-311/18). UK transfers use the Information Commissioner’s Office transfer risk assessment instead.
transfer.nodes.q-safeguard.opts.0.label: Yes — the 2021 standard contractual clauses
transfer.nodes.q-safeguard.opts.1.label: Yes — regulator-approved binding corporate rules for our group
transfer.nodes.q-safeguard.opts.3.label: No practical Article 46 safeguard — check whether an Article 49 exception applies
transfer.nodes.o-scc.title: Use the appropriate transfer contract and assess the destination’s risks
transfer.nodes.o-bcr.title: Use approved binding corporate rules for transfers within the group
transfer.nodes.o-bcr.actions.0: Contact the lead data protection regulator early. Approval requires a substantial review.
transfer.nodes.q-derogation.q: Does one of the limited exceptions in Article 49 apply?
transfer.nodes.q-derogation.help: Article 49 provides exceptions where no adequacy decision or Article 46 safeguard is available. The exceptions are narrow. Guidelines 2/2018 say they must not become the normal legal basis for regular transfers. Assess the conditions of the particular exception for the specific transfer.
transfer.nodes.o-49-c.summary: The contract is between your organization and someone else, but the transfer must be necessary for the benefit of the person whose data is used. This exception is narrowly interpreted.
transfer.nodes.o-49-cli.title: A limited, non-repeated transfer may qualify as a last resort
transfer.nodes.o-no-route.title: You do not have a lawful basis for this transfer
transfer.nodes.o-no-route.summary: The transfer is unlawful without an adequacy decision, an Article 46 safeguard or an applicable Article 49 exception. Stop the transfer until one applies. You could arrange standard contractual clauses and a transfer assessment, or change the service so no restricted international transfer occurs.
transfer.nodes.o-no-route.actions.2: Consider keeping the data in the relevant region, using your own infrastructure, or choosing a processor with no access from outside the permitted area.
transfer.nodes.o-49-cli.actions.3: Tell the people affected about the transfer and the compelling legitimate interests you rely on, in addition to the information required by Articles 13 and 14.
transfer.nodes.q-adequacy.help:
Article 45 allows transfers covered by an adequacy decision: a decision that the destination provides a suitable level of data protection. As of October 2026, the European Commission recognizes Andorra, Argentina, Brazil (since January 2026), Canada (commercial organizations), the Faroe Islands, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Israel, Japan, Jersey, New Zealand, South Korea, Switzerland, the United Kingdom (renewed December 2025), Uruguay, the United States (organizations participating in the EU–US Data Privacy Framework) and the European Patent Organisation. The list can change as decisions are adopted or suspended. Check the European Commission’s current adequacy page before relying on a decision.

UK rules: Schedule 7 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 changes UK GDPR Chapter 5. Under new Articles 45A–45B, the Secretary of State applies a data-protection test when making adequacy regulations: protection must be not materially lower than the UK standard. This differs from the EU’s essentially equivalent protection test. The UK replaces fixed four-year reviews with ongoing monitoring. Check the UK’s own regulations and which amendments have started; the EU and UK lists can differ.

For EU transfers, Schrems II (C-311/18) confirmed the essentially equivalent protection test and invalidated the Privacy Shield. The General Court upheld the successor EU–US Data Privacy Framework in September 2025 (T-553/23); an appeal is pending before the Court of Justice (C-703/25 P). Check its current status before relying on it.
transfer.nodes.o-adequacy.summary:
An adequacy decision allows this transfer without a separate transfer safeguard under GDPR Chapter 5. The European Commission reviews EU adequacy decisions at least every 4 years and can suspend them. The Schrems I and II cases show that courts can invalidate earlier transfer arrangements.

In the UK, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 replaces fixed periodic reviews with ongoing monitoring by the Secretary of State. Check current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance and which amendments have started.
transfer.nodes.o-adequacy.actions.1: Check the European Commission’s current adequacy decisions and the UK’s separate adequacy regulations. They may differ under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, and decisions can be suspended or invalidated, as the Schrems cases demonstrate.
transfer.nodes.o-dpf.summary: The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (July 2023 adequacy decision) covers transfers to US importers self-certified to the framework principles, administered by the US Department of Commerce. The UK has its own Data Privacy Framework Extension (October 2023). Verify the recipient is on the live list before relying on it. Schrems II (C-311/18) invalidated the previous Privacy Shield over US surveillance concerns; the framework added the Data Protection Review Court and Executive Order 14086 to address them. The General Court dismissed the first annulment challenge on 3 September 2025 (Latombe v Commission, T-553/23). Mr Latombe appealed to the Court of Justice on 31 October 2025 (C-703/25 P); the appeal is pending and the framework remains in force meanwhile. The independence and quorum of the US oversight board it relies on (the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board) have also been questioned. Re-verify the framework’s status on the date you rely on this outcome.
transfer.nodes.o-bcr.summary: Binding corporate rules are intragroup data protection policies approved by a data protection regulator that allow transfers within a corporate group. Approval is slow (12–24 months) but durable, and you do not sign standard contractual clauses internally. They are an Article 46 tool, so you must still assess whether the law and practice of each destination let the group members comply, and add supplementary measures where they do not (European Data Protection Board Recommendations 01/2020).
transfer.nodes.o-cofc.actions.3: Assess the destination’s law and practice and add supplementary measures where needed, as for any Article 46 tool (European Data Protection Board Recommendations 01/2020).

special-category.title: Can you use sensitive personal data?
special-category.tag: The EU and UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) give specified sensitive information extra protection. Identify an Article 9 condition as well as an Article 6 legal ground.
special-category.q: What permits this use of health, biometric or other sensitive information?
special-category.nodes.q-type.q: Does the data include any of the sensitive categories in Article 9(1)?
special-category.nodes.q-type.opts.1.label: Yes — biometric data used to identify someone, such as face recognition or identification by fingerprint
special-category.nodes.q-type.opts.2.label: Yes — racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade-union membership
special-category.nodes.o-not-special.title: The extra Article 9 conditions do not apply; you still need an Article 6 ground
special-category.nodes.o-not-special.actions.1: Check whether your analysis reveals sensitive information indirectly. If it does, reassess whether Article 9 applies.
special-category.nodes.o-photo.title: An ordinary photo becomes biometric data under Article 9 when used for unique identification
special-category.nodes.q-health-context.q: Why do you need the health information?
special-category.nodes.q-health-context.help: Article 9(2)(h) covers specified health or social care purposes. Article 9(2)(i) covers public health, and Article 9(2)(j) covers research with safeguards. Explicit consent under Article 9(2)(a) can also permit some uses, but EU or national law, or UK law, can prohibit relying on consent for particular activities.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-h.summary: Article 9(2)(h) permits necessary use for preventive or occupational medicine, assessing working capacity, diagnosis, health or social care, or managing those services. Article 9(3) requires the data to be handled by, or under the responsibility of, a professional bound by an applicable secrecy obligation, or another person bound by such an obligation. In the UK, check Article 9(2)(h) with Data Protection Act 2018 section 10 and Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 2. Section 11(1) supplies the professional-responsibility or equivalent confidentiality requirement.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-h.actions.2: Document the authorizing law and confidentiality requirement. For the EU, identify the EU or national law and Article 9(3) secrecy duty. For the UK, record Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 2 and section 11 of the Data Protection Act 2018.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-i.actions.2: Use only the information necessary for the public health purpose.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-b.actions.3: Keep health information out of human resources systems that do not need it.
special-category.nodes.q-other-9.q: Which condition in Article 9(2) permits this use?
special-category.nodes.q-other-9.help: Article 9(1) prohibits using these categories unless one of the ten Article 9(2) conditions applies, and you still need an Article 6 legal ground as well. Choose the condition that matches the actual activity. In the UK, conditions (b), (g), (h), (i) and (j) also need a basis in Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 (section 10); the others apply directly.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-a.actions.1: Record who agreed, when they agreed and what information they received.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-e.title: The person deliberately made the information public
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-g.actions.2: Use only the personal data necessary for the stated purpose.
special-category.nodes.o-prohibited.title: The proposed use of sensitive data is not permitted
special-category.nodes.o-prohibited.summary: If none of the conditions in Article 9(2)(a)–(j) applies, Article 9(1) prohibits the proposed use. Change the activity so a valid condition applies, obtain valid explicit consent where permitted, avoid using the sensitive information, or stop.
special-category.nodes.o-prohibited.actions.0: Check whether you can achieve the purpose without using the sensitive information.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-g.summary:
Article 9(2)(g) permits processing necessary for substantial public-interest reasons when EU or national law authorizes it. That law must be proportionate, respect data-protection rights and provide suitable, specific safeguards.

In the UK, the conditions are in Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 allows changes to that list by regulations, so check the current Schedule. EU countries have different national rules.
special-category.nodes.o-9-2-g.actions.0: Identify the EU or national law authorizing the processing, or the applicable UK Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1 Part 2 condition.
special-category.nodes.q-other-9.opts.4.label: The person deliberately made this information public — Article 9(2)(e)

adm.title: Can this decision be made automatically?
adm.tag: The EU and UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) set conditions for automated decisions that significantly affect people.
adm.q: Is a fully automated decision permitted, and what protections must you provide?
adm.nodes.q-solely.q: Does a person genuinely review and have the power to change the decision?
adm.nodes.q-solely.help: A decision is solely automated if no person meaningfully reviews it. A person who only approves the recommendation without examining it does not change that. The reviewer needs the authority, skill and relevant information to change the result, including information supplied by the affected person (WP251 rev.01). EU law can also cover a score that someone else relies heavily on for a significant decision, as in SCHUFA Holding (C-634/21). In the UK, check Article 22A and the Information Commissioner’s Office guidance, including whether the Data (Use and Access) Act amendments have taken effect.
adm.nodes.q-solely.opts.0.label: The decision is fully automated, with no human review
adm.nodes.q-solely.opts.1.label: A person approves the automated recommendation without genuinely reviewing it
adm.nodes.q-solely.opts.3.label: A person genuinely reviews every individual decision and can change it
adm.nodes.o-not-art-22.title: Meaningful human review means the Article 22 restriction does not apply
adm.nodes.o-not-art-22.summary: The Article 22(1) restriction does not apply when a person meaningfully reviews the decision. You may still be profiling people: using their data to assess or predict characteristics or behavior. Explain that use and its purpose under Articles 13(1)(c) and 14 and the general fairness and transparency rules. The specific duty to explain automated decision logic in Articles 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g) and 15(1)(h) applies only to the decisions specified in Article 22(1) and (4). WP251 recommends explaining other profiling as good practice.
adm.nodes.o-not-art-22.actions.1: Write down how human review works and who can change a decision.
adm.nodes.q-significant.q: Does the decision change the person’s rights or have a similarly important effect on their life?
adm.nodes.q-significant.help: A legal effect changes a person’s rights or legal position, such as terminating a contract or awarding a benefit. Other significant effects can concern employment, money, essential services, health or education. Ordinary low-impact product advertising usually does not meet this threshold. WP251 explains the distinction.
adm.nodes.o-not-significant.title: The Article 22(1) restriction does not apply to this low-impact decision
adm.nodes.o-not-significant.actions.3: Reassess if the effect becomes more significant, such as when recommendations determine access to a service.
adm.nodes.q-juris.q: Are you assessing the decision under EU rules, UK rules or both?
adm.nodes.q-juris.help: The rules differ. EU Article 22 generally prohibits solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects unless an exception applies. The UK’s Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 replaced Article 22 with Articles 22A–22D, in force since 5 February 2026. Under those provisions, decisions that do not use sensitive data can rely on an Article 6 legal ground with Article 22C safeguards. Decisions using sensitive data face the stricter Article 22B conditions.
adm.nodes.q-uk-scd.q: UK: does the significant decision use any sensitive data covered by Article 9?
adm.nodes.q-uk-scd.help: Under the amended UK rules, Article 22B imposes extra conditions when sensitive data contributes to the decision. Other solely automated significant decisions need an Article 6 ground and the Article 22C safeguards. Article 22A defines meaningful human involvement, and regulations may further explain it. Use the Information Commissioner’s Office guidance for the UK rather than treating EU guidance as binding.
adm.nodes.o-uk-22b.title: UK: sensitive-data decisions need the Article 22B conditions and safeguards
adm.nodes.o-uk-22c.title: UK: the decision may be permitted with a legal ground and safeguards
adm.nodes.o-uk-22c.summary: Since 5 February 2026, a solely automated significant decision that does not use sensitive data can rely on an Article 6 legal ground. Article 22C requires information about the decision and ways for the person to express their views, obtain human intervention and challenge the result. This differs from EU Article 22’s general prohibition with limited exceptions.
adm.nodes.q-22-2.q: EU: which Article 22(2) exception permits the decision?
adm.nodes.q-22-2.help: The EU permits these decisions only where they are necessary to enter into or perform a contract with the person, authorized by EU or national law with safeguards, or based on explicit consent. The UK’s amended rules have a separate assessment, so use the UK questions for a UK-only decision.
adm.nodes.o-22-2-a.title: EU: the decision must be necessary for a contract, with human-review and challenge rights
adm.nodes.o-22-2-a.actions.3: Provide a clear way to request that a person reconsider the decision.
adm.nodes.o-22-2-c.title: EU: obtain explicit consent and provide the Article 22(3) safeguards
adm.nodes.o-22-unlawful.title: EU: the proposed fully automated decision is not permitted
adm.nodes.o-22-unlawful.summary: EU Article 22(1) prohibits the proposed decision unless it is necessary for a contract, authorized by law or based on explicit consent under Article 22(2). Introduce genuine human review or meet an applicable exception before proceeding. The UK has a separate assessment under the Data (Use and Access) Act amendments; do not apply this EU result to a UK-only activity.
adm.nodes.o-22-unlawful.actions.0: Introduce a reviewer with the skill and authority to examine and change the decision.
adm.nodes.o-not-significant.summary:
Article 22(1)’s general restriction does not apply if a decision has neither legal nor similarly significant effects. Using data to evaluate a person may still be profiling under Article 4(4). If it is, you still need an Article 6 legal ground, must explain the profiling under Articles 13 and 14, and must honor the Article 21(2) right to object to direct marketing, including related profiling.

Article 29 Working Party guidance WP251 gives ordinary content personalization as an example below the threshold. Dynamic pricing that effectively excludes someone from a service and advertising that exploits a person’s vulnerabilities can have similarly significant effects. Assess the effects in each case.
adm.nodes.o-not-significant.actions.1: Honor the person’s right to object to direct marketing and related profiling under Article 21(2). That right does not depend on balancing your interests against theirs.
adm.nodes.o-uk-22b.actions.2: Check the current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance on automated decision-making before finalizing the design. Articles 22A–22D have applied since 5 February 2026 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80, commenced by S.I. 2026/82).
adm.nodes.o-uk-22b.actions.3: Data Protection Act 2018 section 14 was omitted on 5 February 2026. Its notification and reconsideration duties apply only to decisions made before that date; do not design new processes around them.
adm.nodes.o-uk-22b.actions.5: Document the analysis, including the Article 22B condition you rely on.
adm.nodes.o-uk-22c.actions.2: Check the current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance on automated decision-making. Articles 22A–22D have applied since 5 February 2026 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80, commenced by S.I. 2026/82).
adm.nodes.o-uk-22c.actions.3: Data Protection Act 2018 section 14 was omitted on 5 February 2026, and the former UK Article 22 was replaced. Those rules apply only to decisions made before that date.
adm.nodes.o-uk-22c.actions.5: Document the analysis and the Article 6 legal ground you rely on.
adm.nodes.o-22-2-b.summary: The law itself must lay down suitable measures to safeguard the person’s rights and freedoms and legitimate interests. Common examples: tax fraud detection statutes; benefits-eligibility automated screening. UK divergence: the UK authorization route is domestic law, not EU or national law. Data Protection Act 2018 section 14 set specific safeguards for law-authorized decisions until it was omitted on 5 February 2026. The UK rules are now in Articles 22A–22D; see the UK branch.
adm.nodes.o-22-2-b.actions.3: UK: apply the Articles 22A–22D safeguards, in force since 5 February 2026. The former Data Protection Act 2018 section 14 duties apply only to decisions made before that date.

children.title: When do you need a parent’s consent?
children.tag: Check the EU and UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the US Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act and California rules.
children.nodes.q-eu-iss.q: Do you offer an online service directly to a child and rely on their consent to use personal data?
children.nodes.q-eu-iss.help: Article 8 concerns consent-based use of children’s data when an information society service, such as an app or online platform, is offered directly to them. It does not change the rules for a different legal ground, such as a contract, legitimate interests or a legal obligation.
children.nodes.q-eu-iss.opts.0.label: Yes — the online service is offered directly to the child and relies on consent
children.nodes.q-eu-iss.opts.1.label: Yes — but we rely on a contract or legitimate interests instead of consent
children.nodes.q-eu-iss.opts.2.label: No — this is not that type of service, such as an offline or business-to-business service
children.nodes.o-eu-not-art8.title: The Article 8 parental-consent rule does not apply to this activity
children.nodes.o-eu-not-art8.summary: Article 8 concerns consent-based online services offered directly to children. For another legal ground, apply Article 6. When relying on legitimate interests, give particular weight to children’s rights. Age-appropriate information and other child-protection rules can still apply.
children.nodes.o-eu-not-art8.actions.1: When assessing legitimate interests, give particular weight to the child’s rights and interests.
children.nodes.q-eu-age.q: How old is the child, and which EU country’s consent age applies?
children.nodes.o-eu-parental.actions.0: Check age before asking the child to consent, and obtain parental authorization where required.
children.nodes.o-eu-self-consent.title: The child can give consent; information must still be appropriate for their age
children.nodes.o-eu-self-consent.actions.0: Check age so children below the applicable threshold are directed to parental authorization.
children.nodes.q-uk-age.q: Does this online service rely on consent from a child under 13 in the UK?
children.nodes.q-uk-age.opts.0.label: The child is under 13 and the service relies on consent
children.nodes.q-uk-age.opts.1.label: The child is 13 or older and the service relies on consent
children.nodes.q-uk-age.opts.2.label: The service does not rely on consent, or is not an online information society service
children.nodes.o-uk-under-13.actions.0: Check age before consent, and obtain parental authorization for children under 13.
children.nodes.o-uk-13-plus.title: UK: children can give their own consent from age 13
children.nodes.o-uk-13-plus.actions.0: Check age so children under 13 are directed to parental authorization.
children.nodes.o-uk-not-art8.title: UK: the age-13 parental-consent rule does not apply to this activity
children.nodes.o-uk-not-art8.summary: The UK Article 8 rule applies to consent-based online information society services offered directly to children. If you rely on another legal ground, assess it under Article 6, giving particular weight to children’s rights when balancing legitimate interests. The Children’s code may still apply if under-18s are likely to use the service.
children.nodes.o-uk-not-art8.actions.1: When assessing legitimate interests, give particular weight to the child’s rights and interests.
children.nodes.o-coppa-yes.title: US: obtain verifiable parental consent and give the required notices
children.nodes.o-coppa-yes.actions.9: Consider an approved safe-harbor program. Such a program creates a presumption of compliance that can still be challenged.
children.nodes.o-coppa-no.title: US: this children’s privacy rule does not currently apply to the service
children.nodes.o-coppa-no.summary: A general-audience service without actual knowledge that it collects data from children under 13 is outside this rule. If you learn that a user is under 13, the obligations apply to that user from that point.
children.nodes.o-coppa-no.actions.1: If you learn that a user is under 13, stop collecting their information or obtain the required parental consent before continuing.
children.nodes.o-coppa-no.actions.3: Check where you advertise. Advertising on children’s sites or services can affect whether your service is considered directed to children.
children.nodes.o-ca-under-13.title: California: a parent or guardian must authorize sale or sharing for children under 13
children.nodes.o-ca-13-15.title: California: people aged 13–15 must opt in to sale or sharing themselves
children.nodes.o-ca-adult.title: California: the usual sale-and-sharing opt-out rules apply from age 16
children.nodes.o-coppa-no.actions.4: Check separate California requirements. Senate Bill 976 on social-media age assurance is under constitutional challenge in NetChoice v. Bonta, and a court has blocked parts of it. Check which provisions can currently be enforced, along with any further California children’s privacy legislation or California Consumer Privacy Act amendments.
children.nodes.o-eu-not-art8.actions.3: Online platforms that are aware with reasonable certainty that a user is a minor must not show them advertising based on profiling with their personal data (Digital Services Act Article 28(2)). This applies whatever the legal ground. Article 28(3) does not require collecting extra data to assess age.
children.nodes.o-eu-parental.actions.4: Online platforms that are aware with reasonable certainty that a user is a minor must not show them advertising based on profiling with their personal data (Digital Services Act Article 28(2), applicable since 17 February 2024). Parental consent does not lift this. Article 28(3) does not require collecting extra data to assess age.
children.nodes.o-eu-self-consent.actions.2: Online platforms that are aware with reasonable certainty that a user is a minor must not show them advertising based on profiling with their personal data (Digital Services Act Article 28(2), applicable since 17 February 2024). The minor’s own consent does not lift this. Article 28(3) does not require collecting extra data to assess age.

breach.title: Who must you tell about a data breach?
breach.tag: Identify who needs notice, the applicable deadlines and what you must record.
breach.nodes.q-incident.help: A personal data breach can involve lost or destroyed data, unauthorized changes, or unauthorized access or disclosure (GDPR Article 4(12)). EU guidance distinguishes harm to confidentiality, accuracy and availability. New York General Business Law §899-aa(1)(c) covers unauthorized access to or acquisition of computerized private information that compromises its security, confidentiality or integrity.
breach.nodes.o-internal-good-faith.title: New York: good-faith employee access is not a breach of the security of the system
breach.nodes.o-no-breach.title: No personal data breach: no breach-notification deadline applies
breach.nodes.o-no-breach.summary: An outage is not a personal data breach if it has not compromised personal data’s confidentiality, accuracy or availability. Check availability carefully: ransomware that prevents access can be a breach even when no data is copied out. Article 32 security duties still apply.
breach.nodes.o-investigate.title: Investigate promptly and record when you became aware of a breach
breach.nodes.o-investigate.summary: Suspicion alone does not establish when the GDPR notification period began. Guidelines 9/2022 allow a short, prompt investigation to establish reasonable certainty that personal data was compromised. Once you have that certainty, assess notification without waiting for the full investigation to finish. The affected jurisdictions and risk determine which duties apply.
breach.nodes.q-territorial.help: More than one notification law may apply to the same breach. Assess each relevant jurisdiction because recipients and deadlines differ.
breach.nodes.q-eu-risk.help: Article 33(1) requires notice to the regulator unless the breach is unlikely to create a risk to people’s rights and freedoms. Article 34(1) requires notice to the affected people only when the risk is high. Guidelines 9/2022 identify six factors: the type of breach; the nature, sensitivity and volume of data; how easily people can be identified; the severity of possible consequences; particular vulnerabilities of the affected people; and how many people are affected.
breach.nodes.o-eu-sa-only.title: Tell the relevant regulator within 72 hours; individual notice is not required here
breach.nodes.q-eu-mitigation.q: Was the data unreadable to the recipient, or have safeguards since removed the high risk?
breach.nodes.q-eu-mitigation.help: Article 34(3) allows exceptions to individual notice. Protection such as effective encryption may have made the data unreadable, or later steps may have removed the high risk. If individual notice would require disproportionate effort, you must use an equally effective public communication instead.
breach.nodes.o-eu-full-notify.title: Tell the regulator within 72 hours and affected people without unnecessary delay
breach.nodes.o-eu-full-notify.actions.5: Preserve evidence of the security measures in place. People may seek compensation under Article 82, and C-340/21 places the burden of showing appropriate Article 32 measures on the controller.
breach.nodes.o-eu-disproportionate.title: Tell the regulator and use equally effective public notice for affected people
breach.nodes.q-uk-risk.help: UK Articles 33–34 use the same risk and high-risk thresholds and the same 72-hour regulator deadline. Report to the UK regulator; the EU system for identifying a lead regulator does not apply. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 did not rewrite these GDPR breach provisions. Separate sector rules may impose other deadlines: EU communications providers have a 24-hour rule under Regulation 611/2013, while the UK Act changes regulation 5A reporting under the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations to 72 hours.
breach.nodes.o-uk-full-notify.title: Tell the UK regulator within 72 hours and affected people without unnecessary delay
breach.nodes.q-ca-breach.q: What type of information about California residents was affected?
breach.nodes.o-ca-pra.title: California: notify residents and assess whether individuals can sue
breach.nodes.o-ca-pra.actions.5: If defending a federal claim, assess whether each claimant has a concrete injury under TransUnion v Ramirez, including whether their information was actually misused or copied out.
breach.nodes.o-ca-1798-82.title: California: the information does not meet this breach-notification law’s definition
breach.nodes.o-ny-no.title: New York: this notification rule does not apply, but security duties remain
breach.nodes.o-ny-good-faith.title: New York: record the decision and tell the attorney general within 10 days if more than 500 residents are affected
breach.nodes.o-ny-notify.title: New York: notify residents and state authorities; regulated financial entities have an additional duty
breach.nodes.o-ny-notify.summary: New York General Business Law §899-aa(2) requires notice as quickly as possible, without unreasonable delay and within 30 days after discovery, subject to a law-enforcement delay. At the same time, notify the state attorney general, Department of State and State Police. Only entities covered by the financial-services rules in 23 NYCRR 500.1 must also notify the Department of Financial Services. The S804 amendment, effective 14 February 2025, requires that notice under §500.17 rather than a second separate filing.
breach.nodes.o-ny-notify.clockSpec.note: The 72-hour financial-services deadline applies only to entities covered by those rules. The resident-notice deadline still requires action as quickly as possible, without unreasonable delay and within 30 days.
breach.nodes.o-il-residents-plus-ag.title: Illinois: notify residents and the attorney general when more than 500 residents need notice
breach.nodes.o-bipa-breach.title: Illinois: assess biometric-data notice duties and possible security-law liability
breach.nodes.o-bipa-breach.actions.5: Assess federal-court standing and the risk of a class action in light of Patel v Facebook, which recognized an injury for biometric notice-and-consent violations without a financial loss.
breach.nodes.o-eu-disproportionate.summary: Under Article 34(3)(c), you may use a public announcement or a similar measure if notifying each person would require disproportionate effort. It must inform people as effectively as individual notices would. The data protection regulator can still require individual notice under Article 34(4).
breach.nodes.o-investigate.actions.3: If EU GDPR Article 33 applies, notify the regulator without unnecessary delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach, unless it is unlikely to create a risk to people’s rights and freedoms. Article 33(4) allows information in phases when necessary. Missing details do not restart the deadline.
breach.nodes.o-eu-full-notify.clockSpec.note: Notify affected people without unnecessary delay under Article 34. There is no fixed statutory date: act as soon as practicable and do not wait for the regulator-notification deadline.
breach.nodes.o-ca-pra.actions.2: Section 1798.150(b) provides 30 days to correct certain violations before a private claim. Improving security after a breach does not count as correcting that breach under this provision.
breach.nodes.o-ca-pra.clockSpec.note: If more than 500 California residents are notified, send the sample notice to the state attorney general within 15 calendar days of the consumer notice under section 1798.82(f). That period begins when you send the notices. Section 1798.82(a)(2)(B) permits exceeding the 30-day limit only for legitimate law-enforcement needs or to determine the breach’s scope and restore system integrity.
breach.nodes.o-internal-good-faith.summary: New York General Business Law section 899-aa(1)(c) excludes good-faith access to or acquisition of private information by an employee or agent for the business’s purposes, provided the information is not used or subject to unauthorized disclosure. If that holds, New York notice is not triggered. This is a New York rule only: under GDPR, access beyond an employee’s authorization can still be a personal data breach, so run the EU or UK branch separately if those people are affected.
breach.nodes.o-eu-no-notify.summary: Under Article 33(1), you do not have to notify the regulator if a breach is unlikely to create a risk to people’s rights and freedoms. Article 33(5) still requires a record of every personal-data breach, including its facts, effects and corrective action, so the regulator can check compliance. European Data Protection Board Guidelines 9/2022 give examples, such as losing an encrypted USB device when the keys are safe and working backups exist; that may not require notification.
breach.nodes.q-ny-mitigation.help: Section 899-aa(2)(a) has an exception for inadvertent disclosures by an authorized person when the business reasonably concludes that misuse or harm is unlikely. Write down that conclusion and keep it for at least 5 years. If more than 500 New York residents are affected, send the written conclusion to the state attorney general within 10 days.
breach.nodes.q-ny-pi.q: Was private information accessed or acquired, or is it reasonably believed to have been accessed or acquired, by a person without valid authorization?
breach.nodes.q-ny-pi.help: New York General Business Law section 899-aa(2) requires notice when private information was accessed or acquired without valid authorization. Signs of access include the information being viewed, communicated with, used or altered; signs of acquisition include it being downloaded, copied, used or in an unauthorized person’s possession (section 899-aa(1)(c)). Section 899-aa(1)(b) defines private information narrowly: personal information plus a sensitive element (Social Security number, license, account number with required security code, biometric, medical, or health-insurance information), or a username or email plus a password or security answer allowing online account access. Public-records data is excluded.

dsar.title: How should you respond to a privacy rights request?
dsar.tag: Identify the requested right, the relevant law and the response deadline.
dsar.q: What does the person want you to do, and when must you respond?
dsar.nodes.q-jurisdiction.q: Which privacy law applies to the request?
dsar.nodes.q-eu-right.help: The GDPR provides rights to access data (Article 15), correct it (Article 16), delete it (Article 17), restrict its use (Article 18), receive a portable copy (Article 20), object (Article 21), and challenge specified automated decisions (Article 22). The amended UK automated-decision provisions are Articles 22A–22D. Article 12 normally requires a response within 1 month. For complex or numerous requests, an extension of 2 further months may be permitted, making 3 months in total; tell the person and explain why within the first month.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-access.title: Provide the personal data and required information within 1 month
dsar.nodes.o-eu-access.clock: 1 month; an extension of 2 further months may be permitted. In the UK, the period may pause for identity checks or clarification.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-erase.title: Delete the data unless an Article 17(3) exception applies
dsar.nodes.o-eu-erase.actions.4: Keep a minimal record showing that deletion occurred, rather than a copy of the deleted data.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-erase.actions.5: Define how deletion requests will be handled in backups and how long backup copies remain.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-port.title: Provide a portable copy when the consent-or-contract conditions apply
dsar.nodes.o-eu-object.title: Stop direct marketing; assess other objections under Article 21
dsar.nodes.o-eu-object.actions.2: Update your records so systems do not resume the activity the person objected to. Article 19 requires recipient notification only if the objection leads to deletion under Article 17(1)(c) or restriction under Article 18, not for the objection alone.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-object.clockSpec.note: An extension of 2 further months may be permitted for complex or numerous requests. Tell the person and explain why within the first month (Article 12(3)). Stop direct marketing immediately; do not wait until the response deadline.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-rect.title: Correct inaccurate personal data and respond within 1 month
dsar.nodes.o-eu-adm.title: EU: check whether the automated decision is permitted and provide the required safeguards
dsar.nodes.o-uk-adm.title: UK: provide automated-decision safeguards and check the extra sensitive-data conditions
dsar.nodes.q-ca-right.q: Which California Consumer Privacy Act right is the person exercising?
dsar.nodes.q-ca-right.help: These rights apply when the California Consumer Privacy Act covers the business and the data. Confirm coverage using the state-law coverage guide. The rights include knowing or accessing data, deletion, correction, a portable copy, opting out of sale or sharing, and limiting certain uses of sensitive personal information. Verification and exceptions depend on the right.
dsar.nodes.o-ca-know.title: California: provide the required access information within 45 days
dsar.nodes.o-ca-delete.title: California: delete the information and tell the relevant recipients to delete it
dsar.nodes.o-ca-delete.summary: Delete the person’s information, direct service providers and contractors to delete it, and notify third parties to whom you sold or shared it unless that is impossible or would require disproportionate effort. Section 1798.105(d) has eight exceptions, covering contract completion, security, debugging, free speech, the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, research, certain internal uses and legal obligations.
dsar.nodes.o-ca-optout.title: California: stop sale or sharing and pass the request to the relevant recipients
dsar.nodes.o-ca-correct.title: California: use commercially reasonable efforts to correct inaccurate information
dsar.nodes.o-ca-limit.title: California: limit use of sensitive information to the permitted purposes
dsar.nodes.o-ca-limit.actions.2: Update the instructions and controls in every system that uses the information.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-access.summary:
Confirm whether you use the person’s data. If you do, provide a copy and explain the purposes, data categories, recipients, retention period or criteria, rights, source of data obtained elsewhere, relevant automated decision-making and safeguards for transfers to other countries. Under Article 15(3), answer electronic requests in a commonly used electronic format unless the person asks otherwise.

For the EU, European Data Protection Board Guidelines 01/2022 say access is the general rule; any restriction needs a specific justification. In the UK, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 provides for reasonable and proportionate searches and pauses while awaiting identity verification or requested clarification. Follow the Information Commissioner’s Office guidance on access requests for those UK rules.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-access.actions.2: UK only: record the start and end of any permitted pause while awaiting identity verification or requested clarification under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
The UK regime differs from the EU GDPR under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Searches need only be reasonable and proportionate (treated as in force from 1 January 2024). The time-limit changes, including pausing while you wait for identity information or clarification, have applied since 5 February 2026. The duty to handle complaints applies from 19 June 2026.
dsar.nodes.q-jurisdiction.opts.1.resultAction: Check the current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance on access requests for how it applies these rules.
dsar.nodes.o-eu-access.actions.8: UK: since 19 June 2026 you must make it easy to complain to you, for example with an electronic complaint form, and acknowledge a complaint within 30 days (Data Protection Act 2018 section 164A).
dsar.nodes.q-adm-regime.help: The regimes diverged on automated decision-making: the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (section 80) replaced UK GDPR Article 22 with new Articles 22A–22D, in force since 5 February 2026.
dsar.nodes.o-uk-adm.actions.3: Check the current Information Commissioner’s Office guidance on automated decision-making. Articles 22A–22D have applied since 5 February 2026 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80, commenced by S.I. 2026/82).

sale-share.title: Are you selling or sharing personal information in California?
sale-share.tag: The California Consumer Privacy Act uses specific definitions of sale and sharing. Check opt-out rights, contracts and protections for children.
sale-share.q: Does giving this information to another organization count as a sale or sharing?
sale-share.nodes.q-business.q: Does your organization qualify as a business covered by the California Consumer Privacy Act?
sale-share.nodes.q-relationship.help: California Civil Code §1798.140 distinguishes service providers, contractors and independent third parties. A service provider or contractor must have a written contract that restricts how it uses the information. The recipient’s actual role and contract affect whether disclosure counts as a sale or sharing.
sale-share.nodes.q-third-purpose.help: A sale involves money or something else of value in return for the information (§1798.140(ad)(1)). Sharing means disclosure for advertising based on a person’s activity across different businesses or services, whether or not money changes hands (§1798.140(ah)(1)). A disclosure can meet both definitions.
sale-share.nodes.q-third-purpose.opts.0.label: We receive money in exchange
sale-share.nodes.q-third-purpose.opts.1.label: We receive something else of value, such as enhanced services
sale-share.nodes.q-third-purpose.opts.2.label: The recipient targets advertising using activity across different businesses or services
sale-share.nodes.q-third-purpose.opts.5.label: The transfer is part of a merger, acquisition or bankruptcy
sale-share.nodes.o-not-sale-not-share.title: The service-provider or contractor exception applies
sale-share.nodes.o-not-sale-not-share.summary: Giving information to a properly contracted service provider or contractor for a business purpose is not a sale under §1798.140(ad) or sharing under §1798.140(ah). The recipient must genuinely work on your behalf, follow the contract’s restrictions and not use the information for its own purposes.
sale-share.nodes.o-not-sale-not-share.actions.2: Require any additional providers the recipient appoints to meet the applicable contract restrictions (§1798.140(ag)(2)/(j)(2)).
sale-share.nodes.o-defective-sp.title: Assess the disclosure as a transfer to an independent third party
sale-share.nodes.o-sale.title: The disclosure counts as a sale
sale-share.nodes.o-share.title: The disclosure counts as sharing for advertising across businesses
sale-share.nodes.o-consumer-directed.title: The person’s deliberate direction can exempt this disclosure
sale-share.nodes.o-consumer-directed.actions.3: Do not obtain agreement through misleading or manipulative interface design. Such consent is invalid under §1798.140(h).
sale-share.nodes.o-optout-signal.title: Passing on an opt-out request does not count as sale or sharing
sale-share.nodes.o-optout-signal.summary: You may send an identifier solely to tell recipients that the person has opted out without making a sale or sharing (§1798.140(ad)(2)(B) and (ah)(2)(B)). This lets the recipients stop the relevant activity.
sale-share.nodes.o-optout-signal.actions.0: Use this exception only to pass on the opt-out request, not for another purpose.
sale-share.nodes.o-mna.title: A transfer in a merger or similar transaction may qualify for an exception
sale-share.nodes.o-affiliate.title: A related company may be covered, but transfers between related companies still need review
sale-share.nodes.o-affiliate.summary: Section 1798.140(d)(2) covers a controlled related company when it shares recognizable branding with a covered business and the business shares consumers’ information with it. That does not clearly make both companies a single business for every purpose. If the recipient is not the consumer-facing business or a properly contracted service provider or contractor, a paid transfer or advertising disclosure could still count as sale or sharing. This interpretation remains unsettled.
