sale-share.nodes.o-not-business.actions.1: Even if the law does not classify you as a business, duties may still apply to employees or through service-provider contracts. Check the duties your contracts create and whether the law’s business definition applies to you.
sale-share.nodes.o-sale.actions.5: Tell third parties that received the sold or shared information about opt-out requests and direct them to comply under Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations section 7026(f)(2). Checking their compliance is recommended practice; this provision does not itself require an audit.
sale-share.nodes.o-sale.actions.6: Conduct and document a risk assessment before selling or sharing (Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations, section 7150(a) and (b)(1)). The rules took effect on 1 January 2026; attestations and assessment summaries for 2026–2027 are due to the California Privacy Protection Agency by 1 April 2028.
sale-share.nodes.o-share.actions.5: Conduct and document a risk assessment before selling or sharing (Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations, section 7150(a) and (b)(1)). The rules took effect on 1 January 2026; attestations and assessment summaries for 2026–2027 are due to the California Privacy Protection Agency by 1 April 2028.

severity.title: How serious is this data breach?
severity.tag: Assess how severe the harm could be and how likely it is. Use the result to inform the EU or UK General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) notification assessment.
severity.nodes.q-scope.help: This guide assesses harm to the people whose data was affected, rather than damage to the organization. That follows GDPR Recitals 75–76 and the ENISA breach methodology. It produces a risk estimate to inform the Article 33–34 notification assessment. Use the breach-notification guide for the actual jurisdiction-specific duties and deadlines. The UK GDPR provisions are materially similar, but EU guidance is not binding in the UK.
severity.nodes.q-sev.help: Assess what affected people could experience, not how large the incident looks to your organization. GDPR Recital 75 includes discrimination, identity theft, fraud, financial or reputational harm, loss of confidential information, reversal of pseudonymization and other significant economic or social harm. Loss of control over personal data also matters. The five severity levels follow NIST SP 800-30. Any references to organizational fines or reputation are background context; they are not what you are scoring.
severity.nodes.q-sev.opts.2.label: Moderate — noticeable but recoverable harm
severity.nodes.o-low.title: Low provisional estimate: confirm the notification decision separately
severity.nodes.o-low.clock: If the 72-hour regulator deadline applies, it begins when you become aware of the breach, not when you finish this assessment.
severity.nodes.o-low.summary: The selected severity and likelihood produce a Low estimate. This can support a documented conclusion that the breach is unlikely to create a risk under Article 33(1), but it does not automatically establish that exception. Article 34 requires notice to affected people where high risk is likely. This is a structured estimate, not the legal notification test. The five-level scales follow NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1; the harms follow GDPR Recital 75; ENISA informs the focus on affected people; and ISO/IEC 27005 informs the risk-matrix approach. The Low, Medium, High and Critical thresholds are this tool’s defaults, not thresholds required by those standards or the GDPR.
severity.nodes.o-low.actions.0: Use the breach-notification guide to decide which notices are required. A Low GDPR estimate does not answer the California, New York or Illinois tests; those laws may still require notice.
severity.nodes.o-low.actions.2: Reassess when the investigation produces new facts, such as confirmed unauthorized copying, decryption or public circulation of data. The estimate remains provisional while relevant facts are unresolved.
severity.nodes.o-low.actions.3: For the affected processing activity going forward, the tool’s Low-band recommendation is to monitor it, document the decision and review periodically. Internal approval does not replace Article 33–34 notification duties.
severity.nodes.o-medium.title: Medium estimate: assess regulator notification now
severity.nodes.o-medium.clock: Record when you became aware of the breach. That starts any applicable 72-hour regulator-notification period.
severity.nodes.o-medium.summary: The selected severity and likelihood produce a Medium estimate. Some risk to people is plausible, so prepare to notify the regulator unless your documented Article 33(1) assessment supports the exception for breaches unlikely to create a risk. Individual notice under Article 34 usually is not required at this level, but assess the data, identifiability, volume and vulnerable people before deciding. This is a structured estimate, not the legal notification test. The five-level scales follow NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1; the harms follow GDPR Recital 75; ENISA informs the focus on affected people; and ISO/IEC 27005 informs the risk-matrix approach. The Low, Medium, High and Critical thresholds are this tool’s defaults, not thresholds required by those standards or the GDPR.
severity.nodes.o-medium.actions.0: Use the breach-notification guide now. Article 33 requires notice without unnecessary delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. Explain a late filing. Reasonable certainty that a breach occurred can establish awareness before the investigation is complete (Guidelines 9/2022).
severity.nodes.o-medium.actions.2: Prepare to reassess individual notice under Article 34 if new facts show that high risk is likely. Any applicable notice must be given without unnecessary delay, subject to Article 34(3).
severity.nodes.o-medium.actions.3: Reassess this provisional estimate as investigation findings become available.
severity.nodes.o-medium.actions.4: For the affected processing activity going forward, reduce risk where reasonably practicable, assign an owner and date, and retain evidence of safeguards. Internal approval does not replace notification duties.
severity.nodes.o-high.title: High estimate: prepare regulator notice and assess individual notice
severity.nodes.o-high.clock: Treat the Article 33 notification period as running from awareness of the breach.
severity.nodes.o-high.summary: The selected severity and likelihood produce a High estimate. Work on the assumption that regulator notice is required under Article 33(1), without unnecessary delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. Assess whether high risk to people is likely under Article 34. Consider the sensitivity of the data, ease of identification, scale and vulnerability. Article 34(3) exceptions can apply where encryption made the data unreadable, later safeguards removed the high risk, or individual notice would require disproportionate effort and an equally effective public communication is used. This is a structured estimate, not the legal notification test. The five-level scales follow NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1; the harms follow GDPR Recital 75; ENISA informs the focus on affected people; and ISO/IEC 27005 informs the risk-matrix approach. The Low, Medium, High and Critical thresholds are this tool’s defaults, not thresholds required by those standards or the GDPR.
severity.nodes.o-high.actions.0: Use the breach-notification guide immediately for the actual EU, UK or US-state duties and deadlines.
severity.nodes.o-high.actions.1: Prepare any required individual notice while preparing the regulator notice. Do not wait until after filing: Article 34 requires action without unnecessary delay.
severity.nodes.o-high.actions.4: Reassess as findings become available. New evidence can increase or reduce the estimate.
severity.nodes.o-high.actions.5: Before continuing the affected processing, add safeguards and reassess, or escalate for documented senior approval. This recommendation concerns processing risk; it does not replace Article 33–34 notification duties.
severity.nodes.o-critical.title: Critical estimate: assume regulator and individual notices are required
severity.nodes.o-critical.clock: Treat the Article 33 notification period and any Article 34 individual-notice duty as requiring action now.
severity.nodes.o-critical.summary: The selected severity and likelihood produce a Critical estimate: severe or hard-to-reverse harm is likely or nearly certain. Work on the assumption that both notices are required: regulator notice without unnecessary delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness under Article 33(1), and clear notice to affected people without unnecessary delay under Article 34(1). Explain any later regulator filing. Check the Article 34(3) encryption, later-safeguard and disproportionate-effort exceptions, although they will rarely fit this level of risk. This is a structured estimate, not the legal notification test. The five-level scales follow NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1; the harms follow GDPR Recital 75; ENISA informs the focus on affected people; and ISO/IEC 27005 informs the risk-matrix approach. The Low, Medium, High and Critical thresholds are this tool’s defaults, not thresholds required by those standards or the GDPR.
severity.nodes.o-critical.actions.0: Use the breach-notification guide now for the relevant jurisdictions and deadlines. If all facts are not available within 72 hours, assess phased notification under Article 33(4).
severity.nodes.o-critical.actions.2: The regulator can order individual notice under Article 34(4). Address that possibility as part of the response.
severity.nodes.o-critical.actions.3: Preserve evidence and document the facts, effects and response under Article 33(5). Expect the records to be examined in a regulatory investigation or legal claim.
severity.nodes.o-critical.actions.4: Reassess when new findings arrive. Document the evidence and reasoning for any reduction as carefully as the original estimate.
severity.nodes.o-critical.actions.5: Do not continue the affected processing unchanged. Reduce the risk immediately or obtain explicit, documented acceptance from accountable leadership. That internal decision does not replace Article 33–34 notification duties.
severity.nodes.o-nopd.title: There is no personal-data harm for this guide to assess
severity.nodes.o-nopd.summary: This guide applies to breaches affecting personal data. An incident affecting only non-personal systems or genuinely anonymous data falls outside that scope. First check logs, backups and support records, which can contain personal data. Preventing access to personal data can itself be a breach, even if no one copied the data out.
severity.nodes.o-processor.title: As processor, tell the controller promptly; do not wait for a risk estimate
severity.nodes.o-processor.summary: Article 33(2) requires a processor to tell the controller without unnecessary delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach. EU guidance interprets that as effectively immediate. The duty has no severity threshold. The controller decides regulator and individual notice under Articles 33(1) and 34; its 72-hour period typically begins when your notice establishes awareness.
severity.nodes.o-processor.actions.0: Tell the controller immediately what you know. Provide further details as they become available.
severity.nodes.o-processor.actions.1: Check the data processing agreement for a shorter notice deadline, required contents and reporting method.
severity.nodes.o-processor.actions.2: Keep sending investigation findings the controller needs, including the nature of the breach, affected categories and approximate numbers, and safeguards taken.
severity.nodes.o-processor.actions.3: You may assess severity on the controller’s behalf and send the provisional estimate with your notice. If the same incident affects data you control for your own purposes, assess that activity separately as controller.
severity.nodes.o-processor.actions.4: Record when you became aware, when you told the controller and when you sent updates. Keep that evidence of Article 33(2) and contractual compliance.
severity.nodes.q-lik-1.q: How likely is further harm to the affected people?
severity.nodes.q-lik-1.help: You assessed severity as Negligible. Now assess the chance of further harm, such as misuse, fraud or wider disclosure. Do not score the chance that the breach happened; its immediate disclosure is already reflected in severity. Evidence supporting Rare includes effective encryption with uncompromised keys, verified non-access, or confirmed deletion or return by a known trusted recipient. Intermediate levels reflect possible or confirmed access without evidence of misuse, considering who may have the data. Almost certain fits confirmed unauthorized copying or information already circulating or being misused. The percentage estimates cover the whole period the data could be exploited, not a fixed year. Guidelines 9/2022 use similar factors.

ai-risk.title: What rules apply to this AI system or model?
ai-risk.tag: Check prohibited uses, high-risk systems, disclosure duties and general-purpose models, including when the EU AI Act requirements apply.
ai-risk.q: What is the classification, and when do its requirements apply?
ai-risk.nodes.q-subject.help:
An AI system is an application, such as a chatbot; a general-purpose AI model is trained software that can be used in many applications.

An AI system (Article 3(1)) is assessed according to what the application is intended to do.

A general-purpose AI model (Article 3(63)) is the trained model used to build different systems. Chapter 5 of the AI Act sets separate rules for these models.

A system built on a general-purpose AI model (Article 3(66)) is assessed as a system. Its classification does not replace the model provider’s separate duties.

Assess each system for its intended purpose. First check the scope rules in Article 2: research-only and pre-market research or development, military or national-security uses, and many free open-source releases are excluded subject to their conditions. Purely personal use is excluded from deployer duties, but the supplier’s duties can still apply. The AI-role guide explains those exceptions.
ai-risk.nodes.q-subject.opts.0.label: An AI application designed for a particular purpose
ai-risk.nodes.q-subject.opts.1.label: An application built using a general-purpose model, such as a chatbot or assistant
ai-risk.nodes.q-subject.opts.1.resultNotes.0: Assess the application separately from the model. Chapter 5 duties remain with the model’s provider. Fine-tuning or substantially modifying the model can make you its provider for that modification; the exact boundary is contested.
ai-risk.nodes.q-subject.opts.2.label: The general-purpose model itself, which developers can use in different applications
ai-risk.nodes.q-prohibited.q: Does the system perform any of the practices prohibited by Article 5?
ai-risk.nodes.q-prohibited.help: The Article 5 prohibitions apply to supplying, putting into service and using systems, including misuse of someone else’s system. Most have applied since 2 February 2025, with a maximum fine of EUR 35 million or 7% under Article 99(3). The 2026 amendments add specified intimate-imagery and child-sexual-abuse-material prohibitions from 2 December 2026. Detecting physical states such as fatigue or pain is not emotion recognition under the Act. Assess that use under the later product-safety or employment questions instead.
ai-risk.nodes.q-annex1.q: Is this a regulated product or safety component that requires an independent conformity assessment?
ai-risk.nodes.q-annex1.help: Article 6(1) requires both conditions: the AI is a product or safety component covered by Annex I legislation, and that product requires a third-party conformity assessment, meaning an independent check against the product rules. Under the 2026 amendments, convenience, user experience, efficiency or quality control alone is not a safety function unless failure could endanger health or safety. An independent assessment required only for non-safety risks, such as radio spectrum, does not count.
ai-risk.nodes.q-annex1.opts.4.label: No — it is not a product or safety component covered by the listed product rules
ai-risk.nodes.q-annex3.help: Assess the purpose described in the system’s instructions and marketing, rather than every possible use. Annex III lists eight areas. Emotion recognition means inferring emotions or intentions from biometric information; detecting fatigue or pain alone does not qualify. Where lawful, emotion-recognition systems are included in Annex III point 1(c). Workplace and education uses are prohibited, subject to the applicable exceptions.
ai-risk.nodes.q-annex3.opts.2.desc: This includes evaluating your own employees. Scoring insider threats or employee misconduct is an employment use under Annex III 4(b), rather than automatically a financial-fraud exception.
ai-risk.nodes.q-annex3.opts.3.desc: The financial-fraud exception concerns that purpose, such as detecting fraudulent transactions. It does not generally exempt scoring the character of staff or customers.
ai-risk.nodes.q-filter.q: Does the system profile people, or can a limited-task exception apply under Article 6(3)?
ai-risk.nodes.q-filter.help: An Annex III listing does not always make the system high-risk. Article 6(3) allows an exception only where the system creates no significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decisions, and one of the four listed conditions applies. A system that profiles people is always high-risk within this Annex III assessment, so that exception is unavailable.
ai-risk.nodes.q-filter.opts.0.resultNotes.0: Profiling prevents use of the Article 6(3) exception.
ai-risk.nodes.q-filter.opts.5.resultNotes.0: The Article 6(3) exception is unavailable when none of its four conditions applies, even if the system does not drive the decision.
ai-risk.nodes.q-transparency.help: Article 50 imposes disclosure duties according to the role and use. Providers have duties for direct AI interactions and generated content. Deployers have duties for specified biometric categorization, emotion recognition, deepfakes and public-interest text. Emotion recognition also needs the Annex III high-risk assessment; Article 50 does not replace it. Inferring emotions will usually involve profiling, and workplace or education prohibitions must also be checked.
ai-risk.nodes.q-gpai.q: Does the general-purpose model meet the conditions for systemic risk?
ai-risk.nodes.q-gpai.help: Systemic risk means risks with potentially widespread effects from a model’s capabilities or use. Every general-purpose model provider has Article 53 duties. Article 55 adds duties for models with high-impact capabilities under Article 51(1)(a), or models designated by the Commission under Article 51(1)(b). Training above 10^25 floating-point operations, a measure of training computation, creates a presumption of high-impact capabilities under Article 51(2). A model can also qualify below that figure if evaluations show capabilities matching the most advanced models.
ai-risk.nodes.q-gpai.opts.0.label: Training exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, or is expected to; or evaluations show capabilities matching the most advanced models
ai-risk.nodes.q-gpai.opts.2.label: Neither condition applies — this is a general-purpose model below the systemic-risk criteria
ai-risk.nodes.o-prohibited.summary: Article 5 prohibits supplying, putting into service and using a system for this practice. These prohibitions have applied since 2 February 2025. Article 99(3) allows fines up to EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. A conformity assessment cannot make the prohibited use lawful. Change the system’s purpose or behavior, or stop the use.
ai-risk.nodes.o-prohibited.actions.1: Check the precise prohibition and its exceptions before redesigning, including the conditions for human-supported criminal-risk assessment, medical or safety emotion recognition, and permitted biometric-dataset filtering.
ai-risk.nodes.o-prohibited-new.title: Specified intimate-imagery and child-sexual-abuse-material uses are prohibited from 2 December 2026
ai-risk.nodes.o-prohibited-new.actions.0: Deployers: do not use a system for the prohibited purpose from 2 December 2026.
ai-risk.nodes.o-rbi.actions.0: If you are not a law-enforcement authority or acting for one, this exception is unavailable. Non-real-time remote biometric identification is separately classified under Annex III point 1 and has Article 26(10) authorization rules.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex1.title: Product-safety high-risk rules apply from 2 August 2028
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex1.summary: The system is high-risk under Article 6(1) when it is a Section A Annex I product or safety component and the product requires third-party conformity assessment. Chapter 3 requirements and Article 16 provider duties are incorporated into the product’s conformity process under amended Article 43(3). The 2026 amendments set 2 August 2028 as the application date. Other AI Act duties may apply earlier or in addition.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex1.actions.1: Also assess Annex III if the intended use falls within one of its areas. Article 6(2) can apply alongside Article 6(1), while conformity assessment still follows the Section A product procedure. The amended text does not expressly resolve all timing questions for dual classifications. Plan for the earlier 2 December 2027 date for Annex III-specific duties, including Article 49(1) registration and applicable Article 26–27 deployer duties.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex1.actions.2: Check Article 50 disclosure duties separately. Relevant AI interactions, generated content, emotion recognition or biometric categorization can require disclosure from 2 August 2026, before the high-risk product date.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex1.actions.3: Deployers must also meet Article 26 oversight, monitoring, logging and worker-information duties. Check whether Article 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment where an Annex III classification and the deployer’s role bring it into scope.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex1.actions.7: If the AI is supplied with the product under the manufacturer’s name, Article 25(3) makes the manufacturer the provider. Use the AI-role guide if the role is unclear.
ai-risk.nodes.o-annex1-b.title: Section B products follow the specified sector-specific rules
ai-risk.nodes.o-annex1-b.actions.0: Follow the legislation for the relevant product sector. Articles 102–109 amend those sector rules, while Article 110 concerns representative actions. The amendments apply from the amending regulation’s entry into force.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex3.title: Annex III high-risk requirements apply from 2 December 2027
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex3.summary: The system is high-risk under Article 6(2). The 2026 amendments move Chapter 3 Sections 1–3, covering classification, requirements and provider/deployer duties, from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. Providers must meet Article 16, including quality management, conformity assessment, CE marking and registration. Deployers have Article 26 duties, and some need an Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment. Other duties can apply earlier.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex3.actions.0: Do not postpone every requirement until December 2027. Article 50 disclosure duties for relevant interactions, generated content, deepfakes, emotion recognition and biometric categorization apply from 2 August 2026. Article 5 prohibitions already apply.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex3.actions.3: Record the dates: Annex III duties apply from 2 December 2027. Systems already marketed before that date generally come into scope only after a significant design change under amended Article 111(2). Annex X large-scale IT components marketed before 2 August 2027 instead have a 31 December 2030 date under Article 111(1). Systems intended for public-authority use must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless.
ai-risk.nodes.o-high-annex3.actions.5: Article 99(4) sets the EUR 15 million or 3% penalty level for specified failures. If the activity becomes a prohibited practice, the EUR 35 million or 7% level applies.
ai-risk.nodes.o-derogation.title: The limited-task exception may avoid high-risk status; the provider must document and register it
ai-risk.nodes.o-derogation.summary: Article 6(3) allows an Annex III system to avoid high-risk classification only if it creates no significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights and the selected condition applies. The provider must document the assessment before marketing or first use under Article 6(4), and register it under Article 49(2). A deployer cannot make this exception decision on behalf of its vendor.
ai-risk.nodes.o-derogation.actions.2: Confirm that the system does not profile people. Any automated evaluation of personal characteristics removes this exception; classifying documents must genuinely differ from scoring the people they concern.
ai-risk.nodes.o-derogation.actions.3: Check both dates. The Annex III classification provisions apply from 2 December 2027, while Article 49 registration provisions apply from 2 August 2026. Prepare the assessment and registration before marketing the system rather than assuming the later date covers both.
ai-risk.nodes.o-derogation.actions.5: Reassess when a feature or use begins influencing decisions. A third party that repurposes a marketed system can become its provider under Article 25(1)(c).
ai-risk.nodes.o-derogation.actions.6: Check Commission guidance and delegated amendments under Article 6(6)–(7), which can change the listed conditions.
ai-risk.nodes.o-transparency.title: Article 50 disclosure duties apply from 2 August 2026
ai-risk.nodes.o-transparency.summary: The system is not high-risk on these answers, but Article 50 still requires disclosure. Providers must tell people they are interacting with AI unless that is obvious, and mark generated audio, images, video or text in a machine-readable way. Deployers must disclose specified emotion recognition or biometric categorization, deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text. These duties apply from 2 August 2026 and must be communicated clearly at the first interaction or exposure.
ai-risk.nodes.o-transparency.actions.5: Article 50 violations can reach the EUR 15 million or 3% fine level under Article 99(4)(g). Reassess if the system is later used for an Annex III purpose.
ai-risk.nodes.o-minimal.title: No additional system-specific requirements on these answers; general duties still apply
ai-risk.nodes.o-minimal.summary: These answers identify no prohibited practice, Annex I or III high-risk use, or Article 50 disclosure requirement. General duties remain: providers and deployers must take measures supporting staff AI literacy under Article 4, applicable since 2 February 2025. The 2026 amendments do not require a guaranteed literacy level. Article 5 prohibitions still restrict how any system may be used. Article 95 codes of conduct are voluntary.
ai-risk.nodes.o-minimal.actions.0: Record the classification and the reasoning for each question, so you can explain the assessment if the intended use changes.
ai-risk.nodes.o-minimal.actions.1: Reassess when the purpose changes. Repurposing a marketed system for an Annex III use can make it high-risk and make the person doing so its provider under Article 25(1)(c).
ai-risk.nodes.o-minimal.actions.3: If the application uses a general-purpose model, its provider still has separate Chapter 5 duties. Use the information supplied under Article 53(1)(b) to support your integration.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai.title: The general-purpose model provider has Article 53 duties
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai.actions.0: Prepare and maintain the four Article 53(1) items: technical documentation, information for system developers, a copyright policy covering reserved rights, and a public training-content summary.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai.actions.3: Use an applicable code of practice to demonstrate compliance until harmonized standards are available. If you do not use a code, Article 53(4) requires an adequate alternative demonstration to the Commission. The Commission’s power to fine model providers (Article 101) has applied since 2 August 2026 (Article 113).
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai.actions.4: Monitor whether training exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, evaluations show the highest-impact capabilities, or the Commission designates the model. Systemic-risk classification adds Article 55 duties and a two-week notification requirement under Articles 51–52.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai.actions.5: If you provide an end-user application using the model, assess that application separately as an AI system. Article 50(2) expressly includes general-purpose AI systems, and putting a system into your own use can count as putting it into service. Giving developers access to the model alone remains a model assessment.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai-systemic.title: Systemic-risk model: Article 53 and 55 duties, plus a two-week notification deadline
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai-systemic.summary: Above 10^25 floating-point operations of training, Article 51(2) presumes high-impact capabilities. Meeting Article 51(1)(a) requires Commission notification without delay and within two weeks under Article 52(1), although Article 52(2) permits a reasoned argument that the model exceptionally poses no systemic risk. Article 55 adds evaluations and adversarial testing, assessment and reduction of EU-wide systemic risks, serious-incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure. The Article 53 open-source exception does not apply.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai-systemic.actions.0: Record the Article 52(1) notification deadline: within two weeks of meeting the condition or knowing it will be met, including during training-run planning.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai-systemic.actions.1: Document Article 55 testing, a maintained register of systemic risks and safeguards, serious-incident reporting arrangements and cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai-systemic.actions.3: Chapter 5 has applied since 2 August 2025. Models already marketed before that date must comply by 2 August 2027 (Article 111(3)).
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai-systemic.actions.5: If you provide an end-user application using the model, assess it separately as an AI system. Giving developers access to the model alone remains a model assessment.
ai-risk.nodes.o-prohibited-new.actions.3: Also check Article 50’s disclosure rules. Lawful synthetic content still requires machine-readable marking from August 2, 2026; legacy systems have until December 2, 2026.
ai-risk.nodes.o-gpai.summary: Providers placing a general-purpose AI model on the EU market must meet Article 53’s duties: technical documentation for authorities meeting Annex XI; information for providers building systems with the model, meeting Annex XII; a copyright-compliance policy that respects rights holders’ reservations under Article 4(3) of the Copyright Directive; and a public, sufficiently detailed summary of training content using the AI Office template. These duties apply from August 2, 2025. Models already on the market before that date have until August 2, 2027 under Article 111(3).

ai-role.title: What is your role under the EU AI Act?
ai-role.tag: Check whether you supply, use, import, distribute or represent an AI system. One organization can have more than one role for the same system.
ai-role.nodes.q-scope.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to this system or model?
ai-role.nodes.q-scope.help: Article 2(1) covers providers supplying systems or putting them into service in the EU, and providers placing general-purpose models on the EU market, wherever the provider is based. It also covers deployers located or established in the EU, and providers or deployers outside the EU when a system’s output is used there. Assess each system separately: the same company may supply one system and use another.
ai-role.nodes.q-hat.q: What does your organization do with this system or model?
ai-role.nodes.q-hat.help: Assess the actual work your organization does; more than one role can apply. A provider develops or commissions a system and supplies it or first uses it under its own name. A deployer uses a system under its authority for professional purposes. An importer first supplies an outside provider’s system in the EU. A distributor resells or otherwise supplies it without being its provider or importer. An authorized representative has a written mandate to act for a provider outside the EU. Articles 3(3)–(8) define these roles. First use for your own purposes counts as putting into service, and free supply can count as making available (Articles 3(10)–(11)). Run this guide for every role that fits.
ai-role.nodes.q-hat.opts.8.label: We supply the general-purpose model itself for developers to use, rather than a finished application
ai-role.nodes.q-deployer-trap.q: Have you changed or rebranded the supplied system in any of these ways?
ai-role.nodes.q-deployer-trap.help: Article 25(1) can make a deployer, importer, distributor or other third party the provider of a high-risk system. It covers the three situations below and brings the Article 16 provider duties. The actual change matters, regardless of the contract’s role label. If the high-risk classification is unclear, complete the AI classification guide first.
ai-role.nodes.q-dist-trap.q: Do you change its branding, software or advertised purpose before supplying it?
ai-role.nodes.q-dist-trap.help: Under Article 25(1), rebranding or substantially modifying a high-risk system, or changing a non-high-risk system’s purpose so it becomes high-risk, can make a distributor its provider. Instructions, advertising and sales material establish intended purpose under Article 3(12). Changing how you market a system can therefore change your role without changing its code. Check the AI classification guide if needed.
ai-role.nodes.q-imp-trap.help: An importer can become a provider by rebranding or substantially modifying a high-risk system, or changing a non-high-risk system to a high-risk purpose. Article 25(1) concerns systems already on the EU market. If you modify it before its first EU supply, Article 3(3) can instead make you the provider of the modified system. The Article 25(2) cooperation rights concern the already-marketed case. Check its high-risk classification separately if unclear.
ai-role.nodes.q-imp-trap.opts.4.resultNotes.0: Article 25(1) does not apply below high-risk classification. However, supplying a system under your own name can still make you its provider under Article 3(3), with relevant Article 50 disclosure duties rather than the Article 16 high-risk duties.
ai-role.nodes.o-provider.summary: You develop or commission the system and supply it or put it into service under your own name or trademark, whether paid or free (Article 3(3)). Your duties depend on the system’s classification, so use the AI classification guide next. Specified provider failures fall within the EUR 15 million or 3% fine level under Article 99(4)(a); prohibited practices have the EUR 35 million or 7% level under Article 99(3).
ai-role.nodes.o-provider.actions.2: If you also supply a general-purpose model, assess that separate role. Chapter 5 model duties under Articles 53–55 have applied since 2 August 2025.
ai-role.nodes.o-provider.actions.6: For tools, services, components or models integrated into a high-risk system, put the Article 25(4) written agreement in place. The 2026 amendments make specified breaches separately subject to fines.
ai-role.nodes.o-provider.actions.7: If you also use the system, you have deployer duties too. Check Article 26 and whether Article 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment.
ai-role.nodes.o-deployer.summary: A deployer uses the system under its authority in a professional setting (Article 3(4)). High-risk Article 26 duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems or 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems under the 2026 amendments. General AI-literacy measures under Article 4 have applied since 2 February 2025. Article 5 also prohibits specified uses, even when the tool itself has lawful purposes. Prohibited use has the EUR 35 million or 7% fine level; specified Article 26 failures have the EUR 15 million or 3% level.
ai-role.nodes.o-deployer.actions.6: Reassess if you rebrand, substantially modify or repurpose the system for a high-risk use: Article 25(1) can make you its provider. If you also import or resell it, assess those roles separately as well.
ai-role.nodes.o-importer.title: You are the importer: check compliance before first EU supply
ai-role.nodes.o-importer.summary: An importer is located or established in the EU and first supplies an AI system bearing the name of a provider outside the EU (Article 3(6)). For high-risk systems, Article 23 requires compliance checks before supply and prohibits supplying a noncompliant or falsified system. Those duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III or 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. Article 5 prohibitions already apply from 2 February 2025, with the new specified imagery prohibitions from 2 December 2026. Specified importer failures have the EUR 15 million or 3% fine level; prohibited practices have the EUR 35 million or 7% level.
ai-role.nodes.o-importer.actions.0: Check Article 5 prohibitions now. They do not wait for the 2027 high-risk requirements.
ai-role.nodes.o-importer.actions.5: If you also use this system in your own operations, assess the deployer role and meet those duties too.
ai-role.nodes.o-distributor.title: You are the distributor: check compliance and stop supplying a noncompliant system
ai-role.nodes.o-distributor.summary: A distributor supplies a system in the EU supply chain without being its provider or importer (Article 3(7)). Article 24 requires specified checks before supply and corrective action when a problem is identified. The high-risk duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III or 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. Specified failures have the EUR 15 million or 3% fine level. Article 5 prohibitions have applied since 2 February 2025, with specified new imagery prohibitions from 2 December 2026; those have the EUR 35 million or 7% fine level.
ai-role.nodes.o-distributor.actions.0: Check the products you supply against Article 5 now; the prohibitions do not wait until 2027.
ai-role.nodes.o-distributor.actions.5: If you also use the system in your own operations, assess and meet the deployer duties.
ai-role.nodes.o-authrep.title: You are the provider’s authorized representative in the EU
ai-role.nodes.o-authrep.summary: You are located or established in the EU and hold a written mandate from a provider outside the EU (Article 3(5)). For high-risk systems, the mandate must cover Article 22(3) tasks, and authorities can address compliance questions to you. Article 54 sets a similar role for general-purpose models. Model mandates have been required since 2 August 2025; the high-risk-system duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III or 2 August 2028 for Annex I. Specified failures have the EUR 15 million or 3% fine level.
ai-role.nodes.o-authrep.actions.4: Put the scope of your mandate in writing and plan the resources needed for 10-year document retention.
ai-role.nodes.o-prodmanuf.title: A Section A product manufacturer can also be the AI provider
ai-role.nodes.o-prodmanuf.summary: Check whether the product legislation is in Section A or Section B of Annex I. For Section A products, supplying or putting a high-risk AI safety component into service under the manufacturer’s name makes the manufacturer its provider under Article 25(3). Article 16 duties apply from 2 August 2028 and are assessed through the product procedure under Article 43(3). Section B products instead follow Article 2(2), which applies Articles 6(1), 60a and 102–112 while product-sector legislation supplies the substantive requirements.
ai-role.nodes.o-prodmanuf.actions.0: Check the product’s Annex I section. The 2026 amendments move machinery from Section A’s former Directive 2006/42/EC entry to Section B’s Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 entry.
ai-role.nodes.o-prodmanuf.actions.2: Plan for 2 August 2028 for Article 6(1) high-risk duties. Check delegated acts under Article 2(13), due by 2 August 2027, which may remove duplicated requirements where product law already provides equivalent protection.
ai-role.nodes.o-flip.title: Your changes make you the system’s provider
ai-role.nodes.o-flip.summary: Under Article 25(1), putting your name on an existing high-risk system, substantially modifying it, or changing a non-high-risk system to a high-risk purpose makes you its provider. You take on Article 16 duties, including conformity assessment, CE marking and registration. Under Article 25(2), the original provider ceases to be provider for that specific system. Rebranding a system that stays below high-risk classification instead needs a separate Article 3(3) assessment; Article 50 duties may apply without the Article 16 requirements.
ai-role.nodes.o-flip.actions.0: Assess the modified or rebranded system’s classification and meet the applicable Article 16 provider duties, including conformity assessment, before further supply.
ai-role.nodes.o-flip.actions.3: Obtain the Article 25(4) written agreement from suppliers of components, tools, services or models used in the high-risk system. Specified failures under Article 25(2) and (4) are separately subject to fines under Article 99(4)(da).
ai-role.nodes.o-downstream.title: You provide the application; the model’s provider has separate duties
ai-role.nodes.o-downstream.summary: Integrating a general-purpose model into a system you supply or first use yourself makes you the resulting application’s provider under Articles 3(11) and 3(68). This is called a downstream provider. Assess the application’s intended purpose and classification. The model’s provider retains Chapter 5 duties for documentation, information for system developers, copyright and the training-content summary. Article 53(1)(b) information is intended to help you comply.
ai-role.nodes.o-downstream.actions.1: Request the Article 53(1)(b) model information. Genuinely free open-source models with public parameters, model weights, architecture and usage information are exempt from the Article 53(1)(a)–(b) package unless they pose systemic risk. For an exempt model, assess capabilities and limitations yourself.
ai-role.nodes.o-downstream.actions.3: If you also use the application, check the deployer duties under Article 26 and whether Article 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment.
ai-role.nodes.o-downstream.actions.5: Reassess a change to a marketed system’s purpose. Making a non-high-risk system high-risk can make you its provider under Article 25(1)(c).
ai-role.nodes.o-excluded.title: An Article 2 exclusion may apply; confirm its conditions
ai-role.nodes.o-excluded.summary: Article 2 excludes specified exclusively military, defense or national-security systems; systems and models developed and used solely for scientific research and development; and pre-market research, testing and development. The conditions matter. A mixed civilian/military use may not qualify, commercial use may end the research exclusion, and testing in real-world conditions is expressly outside the pre-market exclusion.
ai-role.nodes.o-excluded.actions.2: Reassess before marketing the system or testing it with real users. Articles 57–60a separately govern real-world testing.
ai-role.nodes.o-no-nexus.title: These answers do not establish the EU connection needed for this AI Act assessment
ai-role.nodes.o-no-nexus.summary: Article 2(1) can apply through EU supply or first use, an EU-based deployer, or use of a non-EU provider’s or deployer’s output in the EU. None of those connections was selected in this assessment.
ai-role.nodes.o-no-nexus.actions.0: Reassess if EU customers, users or use of the output becomes involved. The output-use rule can apply even without marketing the system in the EU.
ai-role.nodes.o-no-nexus.actions.1: If the system is imported into the EU, assess provider obligations under Article 2(1)(a). For a high-risk system, appoint the Article 22(1) EU representative before supply; Article 23(1)(d) requires the importer to verify the appointment.
ai-role.nodes.o-inhouse.title: An internally built system can make you both provider and deployer
ai-role.nodes.o-inhouse.summary: First use for your own purposes in the EU counts as putting a system into service under Article 3(11). If you build or commission it and use it under your own name, you can therefore be its provider as well as its deployer. You do not need an external customer. Free supply also counts under Article 3(10), so supplying group companies can qualify.
ai-role.nodes.o-inhouse.actions.1: For a high-risk system, meet the provider requirements, including quality management, conformity assessment, declaration, CE marking and applicable registration, plus the Article 26 deployer duties and any Article 27 assessment. The dates are 2 December 2027 for Annex III and 2 August 2028 for Annex I.
ai-role.nodes.o-inhouse.actions.3: If you substantially customize a vendor’s system, assess Article 25(1). The original provider may owe documentation, limitation information and testing access under Article 25(2). A system built from scratch has no original provider with those cooperation duties.
ai-role.nodes.o-inhouse.actions.4: If you use someone else’s general-purpose model, request Article 53(1)(b) documentation. For a high-risk system, obtain the Article 25(4) written agreement with the model supplier.
ai-role.nodes.o-gpai-provider.title: The general-purpose model provider has separate Chapter 5 duties
ai-role.nodes.o-gpai-provider.summary: Supplying a general-purpose model under Article 3(63) has duties separate from an application built with it. Chapter 5, including Articles 53–55, has applied since 2 August 2025. Article 53 requires technical documentation for authorities, information for system developers, a copyright policy addressing reserved text-and-data-mining rights, and a public training-content summary using the AI Office template. The Commission’s power to fine model providers (Article 101) has applied since 2 August 2026 (Article 113).
ai-role.nodes.o-gpai-provider.actions.2: Check Article 53(2): qualifying free open-source models are exempt from the Article 53(1)(a)–(b) documentation duties, not the copyright policy or training-content summary. Models with systemic risk cannot use this exception.
ai-role.nodes.o-gpai-provider.actions.3: Training above 10^25 floating-point operations, a measure of computation, or capabilities matching the most advanced models can create systemic-risk duties. Notify the Commission within two weeks and meet Article 55. Use the AI classification guide for the detailed assessment.
ai-role.nodes.o-gpai-provider.actions.4: If you also provide an end-user application using the model, assess it separately as a system. First use for your own purposes also counts as putting into service. Providing developers access to the model alone remains a model assessment.
ai-role.nodes.q-hat.opts.6.label: We manufacture a physical product, such as a toy, elevator or medical device, supplied under our name with this AI as a safety component
ai-role.nodes.o-provider.actions.0: Classify the system. Article 5’s prohibitions have applied since February 2, 2025; the new prohibitions on nonconsensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material apply from December 2, 2026. High-risk duties begin December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2, 2028 for Annex I product systems, following the 2026 Digital Omnibus changes. Article 16 duties include risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logs, information for deployers, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, a quality management system, conformity assessment, CE marking and registration.
ai-role.nodes.o-prodmanuf.actions.3: If the AI safety component is supplied under the AI supplier’s name instead of yours, that supplier is its provider. Apply Article 25(4)’s written-agreement requirements to the responsibilities shared between you.
ai-role.nodes.o-inhouse.actions.0: Use the AI risk guide to classify the system. Internal credit-scoring, recruitment and fraud-scoring systems can fall within Annex III; assess the specific intended purpose.
ai-role.nodes.o-excluded.actions.1: Free and open-source AI systems are also outside scope (Article 2(12)) unless placed on the market or put into service as high-risk systems, or falling under Article 5 (prohibited practices) or Article 50 (transparency). This exclusion covers AI systems, not general-purpose AI models; open-source models get only the narrower relief in Articles 53(2) and 54(6).

us-applicability.tag: Check whether a state’s privacy law covers your organization and use of data.
us-applicability.nodes.ca-nexus.q: Does the person or organization do business in California?
us-applicability.nodes.ca-nexus.help: The California Consumer Privacy Act does not define doing business; evidence usually includes customers, sales, deliveries, staff, offices or contracts in California. Use the actual person or organization and processing in this assessment. A website being technically reachable is not by itself proof of the stated business or targeting test. Who counts as a consumer in the later questions: California residents, including employment and business-contact data; the transaction-count condition also counts households. It counts buying, selling or sharing, not processing alone.
us-applicability.nodes.ca-nexus-unknown.missingFacts.0.fa: Does the person or organization do business in California? Record resident reach, contracts, delivery and targeting evidence.

This comparison covers 20 state laws in effect by September 22, 2026. Future changes are labeled with their start dates. Profiling means using automated processing to assess or predict a person’s characteristics or behavior.
us-divergence.nodes.ca-enforcement.title: California: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ca-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The CPPA and Attorney General enforce the CCPA. There is no mandatory general period to correct a violation before enforcement; any CPPA opportunity is discretionary with no fixed statutory duration.
us-divergence.nodes.ca-enforcement.actions.0: Correct the violations without assuming a 30-day regulatory grace period; that general requirement ended January 1, 2023.
us-divergence.nodes.ca-enforcement.actions.1: If the CPPA grants time to correct the violation, follow its terms and preserve evidence of the corrective work. Keep the separate breach-claim notice rule distinct.
us-divergence.nodes.co-enforcement.title: Colorado: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.co-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Attorney General and district attorneys enforce the CPA. The general right to correct a violation before enforcement expired, but a conditional 60-day right remains for three minors provisions until repeal effective December 31, 2026.
us-divergence.nodes.co-enforcement.actions.0: Identify the specific alleged provision. For §§6-1-1305.5, 1308.5 or 1309.5, a violation that can be corrected triggers notice and 60 days after receipt under the current rule.
us-divergence.nodes.co-enforcement.actions.1: For other CPA duties, do not assume a mandatory opportunity to correct a violation before enforcement. Keep the minors-only repeal date separate from implementation deadlines.
us-divergence.nodes.ct-enforcement.title: Connecticut: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ct-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Attorney General enforces the act. Correction opportunities have been discretionary since January 1, 2025; current law does not guarantee the former 60-day window.
us-divergence.nodes.ct-enforcement.actions.0: Treat any opportunity to correct a violation and deadline as matters to establish with the Attorney General; do not assume that a notice automatically gives 60 days.
us-divergence.nodes.ct-enforcement.actions.1: Preserve the alleged provisions, notice and corrective work evidence. The expired rules for correcting violations before enforcement does not postpone current statutory duties.
us-divergence.nodes.de-enforcement.title: Delaware: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.de-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Department of Justice enforces the act. Correction opportunities are discretionary from January 1, 2026; the former mandatory 60-day regime has expired.
us-divergence.nodes.de-enforcement.actions.0: Do not rely on the 2025 right to notice and an opportunity to correct a violation. Establish any offered correction terms and deadline with the Department of Justice.
us-divergence.nodes.de-enforcement.actions.1: Record the notice, alleged provisions and completed corrective work; the statute's current discretionary language does not guarantee 60 days.
us-divergence.nodes.fl-enforcement.title: Florida: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.fl-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Department of Legal Affairs may grant 45 calendar days after written notice to correct the violation a violation. This is discretionary and unavailable for the statutory known-child cases.
us-divergence.nodes.fl-enforcement.actions.0: For an offered period to correct a violation, complete corrective work within the granted 45 calendar days and provide proof satisfactory to the Department.
us-divergence.nodes.fl-enforcement.actions.1: Check whether the allegation involves a known child or guidance denies a future opportunity to correct a violation. Neither a consumer-response deadline nor the act's start date supplies extra correction time.
us-divergence.nodes.in-enforcement.title: Indiana: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.in-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Attorney General must give 30 days' written notice before enforcement action. Correction plus the required written statement prevents that action, subject to continued violations or a breached statement.
us-divergence.nodes.in-enforcement.actions.0: Record the deadline for the 30-day period on the Attorney General's written notice and correct the violations each identified violation.
us-divergence.nodes.in-enforcement.actions.1: Provide the express written statement confirming correction and preventive actions; preserve evidence supporting it and monitor for recurrence.
us-divergence.nodes.ia-enforcement.title: Iowa: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ia-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Attorney General must provide 90 days' written notice. Correction and the required written assurance prevent that action, unless violations continue or the assurance is breached.
us-divergence.nodes.ia-enforcement.actions.0: Calendar the 90-day enforcement window from the Attorney General's written notice, separately from consumer-request deadlines.
us-divergence.nodes.ia-enforcement.actions.1: Complete the corrective work and provide an express written statement that the violations are corrected and no further such violations will occur; retain supporting evidence.
us-divergence.nodes.ky-enforcement.title: Kentucky: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ky-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Attorney General must give 30 days' written notice. Timely correction and a written assurance prevent the subsection (3) damages action, subject to recurrence or a breached assurance.
us-divergence.nodes.ky-enforcement.actions.0: Record the 30-day deadline in the Attorney General's written notice, correct the identified violation and supply the required express written assurance.
us-divergence.nodes.ky-enforcement.actions.1: Preserve evidence of correction and prevent recurrence. Keep the statutory protection scoped to the damages action described in §367.3627(3).
us-divergence.nodes.md-enforcement.title: Maryland: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.md-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Consumer Protection Division may offer correction for violations occurring on or before April 1, 2027. If it gives notice, at least 60 days after receipt must be allowed.
us-divergence.nodes.md-enforcement.actions.0: Record when the alleged violation occurred and whether the Division granted a opportunity to correct a violation; notice is discretionary.
us-divergence.nodes.md-enforcement.actions.1: If notice is granted, record its specified deadline, allowing at least 60 days after receipt, and document the completed correction.
us-divergence.nodes.mn-enforcement.title: Minnesota: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.mn-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: The Attorney General enforces the act. The mandatory warning-letter and 30-day procedure for correcting a violation before enforcement expired January 31, 2026.
us-divergence.nodes.mn-enforcement.actions.1: Keep any agreed corrective work deadline separate from the act's implementation dates and preserve proof of completed corrective work.
us-divergence.nodes.mt-enforcement.title: Montana: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.mt-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Montana's Attorney General enforces the Act. Current §30-14-2817 does not provide a guaranteed period to correct a violation before enforcement; the former 60-day opportunity is not a current entitlement.
us-divergence.nodes.mt-enforcement.actions.1: Do not assume a fresh 60-day implementation period or delay correction while waiting for a notice offering an opportunity to correct a violation.
us-divergence.nodes.ne-enforcement.title: Nebraska: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ne-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Nebraska requires a 30-day pre-action notice and opportunity to correct a violation. Timely correction must be backed by written statements and supporting evidence; fixing the issue alone does not satisfy the statutory conditions for correcting a violation and avoiding enforcement.
us-divergence.nodes.ne-enforcement.actions.1: Within that period, correct the identified violation and provide the Attorney General a written statement confirming correction with supportive documentation, plus an express written commitment not to commit such a violation after correction.
us-divergence.nodes.ne-enforcement.actions.2: Keep this period to correct a violation before enforcement separate from consumer-request deadlines and the law's implementation date.
us-divergence.nodes.nh-enforcement.title: New Hampshire: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.nh-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: New Hampshire's 60-day opportunity to correct a violation is discretionary from January 1, 2026. It is not an automatic grace period: the Attorney General must first grant the opportunity by issuing the relevant notice.
us-divergence.nodes.nh-enforcement.actions.0: Identify whether the Attorney General has issued a notice offering an opportunity to correct a violation; if so, record receipt and the sixty-day deadline for correcting the violation.
us-divergence.nodes.nh-enforcement.actions.1: Address the alleged violation and document the factors relevant to the Attorney General's discretion: violation count, person or organization size/complexity, processing, public injury, safety, and human or technical error.
us-divergence.nodes.nj-enforcement.title: New Jersey: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.nj-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: New Jersey's temporary 30-day opportunity to correct a violation has expired. The statute's month-based cutoff was July 1, 2026, so current enforcement should not assume an automatic notice offering an opportunity to correct a violation.
us-divergence.nodes.nj-enforcement.actions.0: Route enforcement correspondence to the legal owner without assuming the former thirty-day protection from enforcement after correcting a violation.
us-divergence.nodes.or-enforcement.title: Oregon: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.or-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Oregon no longer guarantees the former 30-day opportunity to correct a violation. General protection ended at the start of 2026, and the narrow temporary broadcaster exception was repealed July 1, 2026.
us-divergence.nodes.or-enforcement.actions.0: Treat current enforcement correspondence as requiring prompt legal review; do not assume a statutory thirty-day correction before an action.
us-divergence.nodes.or-enforcement.actions.2: Keep past rules for correcting violations before enforcement separate from current compliance duties and consumer-request deadlines.
us-divergence.nodes.ri-enforcement.title: Rhode Island: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ri-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Rhode Island's comprehensive privacy chapter gives the Attorney General sole enforcement authority and does not provide a guaranteed period to correct a violation before enforcement.
us-divergence.nodes.ri-enforcement.actions.0: Route an alleged violation or enforcement notice to the legal owner promptly instead of applying another state's thirty- or sixty-day rule for correcting violations before enforcement.
us-divergence.nodes.tn-enforcement.title: Tennessee: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.tn-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Tennessee requires 60 days' written pre-action notice. The enforcement bar depends on timely correction and an express written assurance to the Attorney General and Reporter.
us-divergence.nodes.tn-enforcement.actions.0: Record the written notice, specific allegations and sixty-day period to correct a violation.
us-divergence.nodes.tn-enforcement.actions.1: Within the period, correct the noticed violation and provide an express written statement that the alleged violations are corrected and no such further violations will occur.
us-divergence.nodes.tn-enforcement.actions.2: Maintain the corrective controls: continued violations or breach of that statement can permit an action. This period to correct a violation is separate from implementation and consumer-response deadlines.
us-divergence.nodes.tx-enforcement.title: Texas: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.tx-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Texas requires a 30-day opportunity to correct a violation before enforcement action, with the required written statements and evidence of correction. Consumer notification and supporting documentation are part of the statutory conditions.
us-divergence.nodes.tx-enforcement.actions.0: Record the Attorney General's written notice, alleged provisions and thirty-day period; correct the identified violation within that period.
us-divergence.nodes.tx-enforcement.actions.1: Provide a written statement confirming correction; notification to the affected consumer if that consumer's contact information was made available to the person; supportive documentation showing correction; and necessary internal-policy changes to prevent such further violations.
us-divergence.nodes.tx-enforcement.actions.2: Preserve proof of each condition. The process for correcting a violation before enforcement does not postpone ordinary compliance or consumer-response duties.
us-divergence.nodes.ut-enforcement.title: Utah: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.ut-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Utah requires notice and a 30-day opportunity to correct a violation before the Attorney General's referred enforcement action. The deadline runs after receipt, and a written statement confirming correction and promising that the violation will not recur is also required.
us-divergence.nodes.ut-enforcement.actions.1: Correct the violation within thirty days after the day of receipt and provide an express written statement that the violation is corrected and no further occurrence of the corrected violation will happen.
us-divergence.nodes.ut-enforcement.actions.2: Keep the Division referral, notice and proof of correction together. Continued violations after correction can permit enforcement; consumer-response and future implementation dates remain separate.
us-divergence.nodes.va-enforcement.title: Virginia: correcting violations and enforcement
us-divergence.nodes.va-enforcement.summary: Because you confirmed that the law generally covers this activity: Virginia requires 30 days' written pre-action notice. Timely correction plus an express written statement to the Attorney General prevents the action under the stated statutory conditions.
us-divergence.nodes.va-enforcement.actions.1: Within the period, correct the noticed violation and provide an express written statement that the alleged violations are corrected and no further violations will occur.
us-divergence.nodes.va-enforcement.actions.2: Maintain the corrective controls: a continued violation or breach of the statement can permit enforcement. This is an period to correct a violation before enforcement, not an implementation extension or consumer-response deadline.
